(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## 30e562b4-7e14-433d-b759-3d1b85dd1bc2
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. ## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. In-chat only -- never saved to a file; no reflective questions. LifeHQ-Mark is excluded by a global deny rule.

## APR Skills

### Blog Critique
**Purpose:** Critiques a draft blog post against Mark's established writing style. Flags tone slips, off-voice vocabulary, and clunky sentence structures, plus a logic and content gap analysis and a dependency-order (information-DAG) check that section order grounds each term/concept before a later section leans on it. No rewrites. When the draft is a Markdown file, delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat bullets are the fallback for pasted text.
**Triggers:** "critique this blog post", "review my blog draft", "blog critique", "voice check my blog", "does this blog sound like me"
**File:** `Skills/APR/blog-critique/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format)

### Competitive Landscape
**Purpose:** Competitive analysis frameworks (Porter's Five Forces, Blue Ocean, positioning maps) tailored for APR's Scrum/Agile training and GenAI-for-business-agility market. Writes new analyses to `APR/Analytics/`.
**Triggers:** "analyze competitors", "competitive landscape", "identify differentiation", "market positioning", "Porter's Five Forces"
**File:** `Skills/APR/competitive-landscape/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Existing APR competitive docs in `APR/Analytics/` (e.g. `genai-course-competitive-analysis.md`)

### Content Performance
**Purpose:** Analyze APR content performance across social media, email newsletters, and website traffic. Reads raw data from the Astro repo (`agile-pain-relief-astro/analytics/`), writes a single live snapshot to `APR/Analytics/content-performance-snapshot.md` (overwrite, not dated).
**Triggers:** "content performance", "analyze my content", "how are my posts doing", "newsletter engagement", "which topics perform best", "social to website traffic"
**File:** `Skills/APR/content-performance/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Bash access to Astro repo analytics folder, `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` for matching newsletter content

### Linkedin Style
**Purpose:** Two modes for Mark's LinkedIn presence. Review mode (default) critiques draft posts against Mark's voice and LinkedIn-specific conventions (length, hooks, emoji, hashtags, external links) and delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup on a Markdown file (chat is the fallback for pasted text). Draft mode generates 2-3 complete draft-post options from a topic Mark gives or from his blog/glossary/newsletter content, built mostly by reusing his own sentences and phrasing from the source so the draft already sounds like him and he can edit rather than start blank. Covers Scrum/Agile posts, GenAI/LLM posts (skeptical-pragmatist lean), personal posts, and business announcements.
**Triggers:** "review this LinkedIn post", "critique my post", "LinkedIn style", "LinkedIn rubric", "post review", "does this post sound like me", "voice check on this post", "draft a LinkedIn post", "give me LinkedIn post ideas", "draft LinkedIn options", "LinkedIn post from this newsletter", "draft some posts on"
**File:** `Skills/APR/linkedin-style/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format); reference newsletters in `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` optional for calibration; cross-platform emoji policy in `_social-posting-conventions.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo)

### Newsletter Reading Recap
**Purpose:** Builds the "Mark's Reading Rabbit Hole" section for the newsletter — a paste-ready Markdown list of what Mark read since the last issue, linked to originals, with neutral one-line descriptions. Papers and PDFs lead; archived-without-highlights items are demoted to a short trailing list. Window defaults to "since the last newsletter" (auto-detected from the Newsletter folder). Skips any article already featured in the reading section of the last 15 issues (exclusion set derived from the newsletter files themselves, reading-section links only, URL-normalized); the window can widen further back since repeats are filtered. Read-only and print-to-chat only; never edits the newsletter file.
**Triggers:** "reading recap for the newsletter", "reading rabbit hole", "what should go in the newsletter reading list", "newsletter reading section"
**File:** `Skills/APR/newsletter-reading-recap/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Readwise CLI (preferred) or Readwise MCP; reads `Skills/Readwise/readwise-cli/SKILL.md` for command reference

### Newsletter Reviewer
**Purpose:** Reviews and critiques draft newsletters against Mark's authentic voice, tone, and style guidelines. Produces a structured critique with anti-pattern detections, terminology checks, a provisional subject-line check (filename-derived line plus any `// Subject A:` / `// Subject B:` A/B variants), and priority fixes. When the draft is a Markdown file, delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat critique is the fallback for pasted text.
**Triggers:** "review my newsletter", "critique this draft", "does this sound like me", "voice check", "newsletter rubric", "style check", "review my subject line", "subject line check"
**File:** `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format)

### Reshare Queue Tune
**Purpose:** Quarterly performance re-tier of the social-media reshare queue in `complete-social-media-calendar.md`. Measures how each already-posted queue item performed when reshared (PostHog `archive-reshare` attribution, LinkedIn-weighted, normalised to clicks-per-reshare) plus social engagement from `history.json`, then proposes tier moves (promote to TIER 2 / demote / retire) and surfaces high-traffic pages not yet queued. This is the **major** update; the monthly **minor** update (curate newly published posts/glossary via `calendar-audit`) does not need this skill. Approval gate before editing; refreshes the header with `calendar-audit --write`.
**Triggers:** "tune the reshare queue", "re-tier the calendar", "which reshares are working", "reshare queue review", "quarterly social queue update"
**File:** `Skills/APR/reshare-queue-tune/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `apr-weekly-analytics` (data refresh), `apr-content-performance` (optional context), `calendar-audit` in the `social-media-posting` repo, Bash access to Astro repo analytics; pairs with `quarterly-review`

### Seo Audit
**Purpose:** Diagnose structural SEO issues on agilepainrelief.com. Five-section audit framework (Crawlability, Technical, On-Page, Content/E-E-A-T, Authority) tightened for an Astro content/blog site. Produces a prioritised findings report at `APR/Analytics/seo-audit-YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Findings only, no auto-fix.
**Triggers:** "audit my SEO", "SEO audit", "why am I not ranking", "SEO health check", "my traffic dropped", "check my technical SEO"
**File:** `Skills/APR/seo-audit/SKILL.md`

### Weekly Analytics
**Purpose:** Orchestrate the weekly analytics loop — run `npm run scrape` and `npm run posthog-export` in the Astro repo, invoke `apr-content-performance` to regenerate the live report, flag experiment follow-ups, capture tasks to OmniFocus.
**Triggers:** "run weekly analytics", "refresh analytics", "pull analytics", "weekly data pull"
**File:** `Skills/APR/weekly-analytics/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `apr-content-performance`, `omnifocus-capture`, `omnifocus-workflow`, Bash access to Astro repo

## Writing Skills

### Criticmarkup Editing
**Purpose:** Default delivery format for feedback on Mark's Markdown writing -- annotate the file in place with CriticMarkup (comments `{>>Claude: …<<}`, additions `{++…++}`, deletions `{--…--}`, substitutions `{~~old~>new~~}`, highlights `{==…==}`), reviewed in Obsidian's Track Changes side panel. The voice rubrics decide WHAT to flag; this skill decides HOW to deliver it. Always delivers the full markup pass in one go (no section-by-section chunking; the CLAUDE.md chunked-review preference does not apply to CriticMarkup passes). Applies to all writing types including sales/marketing copy. Never rewrites Mark's prose outside a markup wrapper. Falls back to chat bullets for pasted (non-file) content.
**Triggers:** "edit this", "mark up my draft", "track changes", "use CriticMarkup", "suggest edits inline", "give me feedback on my writing"
**File:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Obsidian Track Changes plugin (`.obsidian/plugins/track-changes/`); read alongside the relevant voice rubric (apr-blog-critique, apr-newsletter-reviewer, apr-linkedin-style, Marketing/copy-editing, storybrand-messaging)

### Email Voice
**Purpose:** Mark's email writing voice, for a dictation tool to draft emails that sound like him. Covers shared structure, professional vs personal registers, mechanics, and a dictation correction/vocabulary list. Built from analysis of 50+ sent emails.
**Triggers:** "draft an email", "write this email in my voice", "email in my voice", "make this email sound like me", "reply to this email as me"
**File:** `Skills/Writing/email-voice/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** None

---

## Communication Skills

### Drafts Inbox
**Purpose:** Triages everything in the Drafts inbox (no longer keyed to a "cowork" tag), classifies each item, takes action, and archives when done so the inbox stays the unprocessed queue. For a large backlog, asks how far back to go and filters by `modificationDate`. Tasks route to `omnifocus-capture`.
**Triggers:** "check my Drafts inbox", "process my inbox", "what's in Drafts", "triage my Drafts inbox", "drafts inbox triage"
**File:** `Skills/Comms/drafts-inbox/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Drafts MCP connector; `Skills/OmniFocus/capture/SKILL.md` (for task capture)

### Gmail Triage
**Purpose:** Recommend a triage plan for the Gmail inbox via the Gmail MCP. Classifies each thread into one of four actions — reference (file under existing label), reply-needed (draft suggestion only), trash, or archive (remove INBOX, keep in All Mail for records) — with a Task overlay for emails that imply an OmniFocus action. # Drafts Inbox

Triage the items sitting in the Drafts **inbox** — your capture-to-action pipeline. Archiving each item when it's handled means the inbox itself is the "unprocessed since last run" queue; there's no separate timestamp to track.

## When to Use

Use this skill at the start of a session or whenever you want to process items you've captured throughout the day via Drafts on iPhone, Apple Watch, or Mac.

## Prerequisites

- Drafts MCP connector must be set up.

## Instructions

1. Read the inbox with `drafts_get_drafts` (`folder: "inbox"`). This returns summaries only (title, dates, flags, tags), not full content.
2. **Check the volume first.** If the inbox is large (more than ~20 items, i.e. a backlog rather than a session's worth), don't try to process everything blindly. Report the count and date range, and ask how far back to go (e.g. this month, last 3 months, flagged only, or the whole backlog). Default to the most recent window.
   - The MCP returns the full inbox; use the `modificationDate` field to filter to the chosen window yourself. `drafts_get_drafts` also accepts `modifiedAfter` / `flagged` to narrow the pull.
3. Present a numbered list of the in-scope items with a brief preview of each.
4. For each item, pull its full content with `drafts_get_draft` (the summary title is truncated), classify it, and take the appropriate action:

| Type | Action |
|------|--------|
| **Task or to-do** | Capture to OmniFocus via `omnifocus-capture` (inbox by default). Flag if urgent. |
| **Writing idea (substantial)** | Create a Writing Task in `APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/` (frontmatter: `status`, `priority`, `dateCreated`/`dateModified`, `tags: [task]`, `ContentType: Blog`/`Newsletter`/`Glossary`). |
| **Content hook (one-liner)** | Add to the running `APR/Efforts/Content Ideas.md` note. |
| **Research request** | Do the research and report findings. |
| **Quick instruction** | Execute the instruction (file a note, move a file, look something up). |
| **Question** | Answer the question. |
| **Reference / clipping** | File it where it belongs (vault note, DevonThink, etc.) or note that it's already captured elsewhere. |
| **Unclear** | Ask for clarification before acting. |

5. After processing each item, archive the draft with `drafts_archive`.
6. Report what was done: "[N] items processed. [Brief summary of actions taken.]"

## Rules

- Process items one at a time. Don't batch everything silently. (For a large backlog, a grouped proposal with a per-item action is fine, but get approval before archiving or capturing anything.)
- When an item is ambiguous, ask rather than guess.
- Archive each draft only after it's been fully processed — the archive is what marks it "done," so never archive something you skipped.
- If an item requires a tool you don't have access to, note it and move on (leave it in the inbox).
- Confirm before deleting; default to archive, not trash.

---

*Started with the Robot Assistant Field Guide Starter Kit. Customized in Video 6 via the assembler. Updated 2026-06-28 to triage the whole inbox instead of a "cowork" tag.*

  "id": "860BEADB-FDFF-4E57-9F41-796D9864A4D1",
  "title": "Reshuffle",
  "content": "Reshuffle

The music industry is a good example of the change that is being unleashed by AI.

Music came in albums and required a record company's backing because of the pressing costs for the vinyl and the need for distribution network.

Digital music reduces those costs and so albums become less important and singles more important.

Spotify, Apple Music et al, become arise because they become the way people find music.

In the process much of the old music industry died.
--
Using Shein, with all of it's flaws, as another example - the work heirarchy has been completely inverted. There aren't long meetings about reducing risk. There aren't seasonal cycles, they run small experiments, if an item takes off they do more, if it fails they look for another.experiment.

There are no silos and limited coordination overhead.

Ignoring the ethical and environmental implications of the way they do business, they're a very agile organization.

Shein's success isn't about doing individual tasks faster, but deliver the outcomes that the audience wants sooner.
--
## Ch 5 Rebundling the Job
Core claim - in a world where everyone has access to the same knowledge, there is knowledge overwhelm.

The promise of good taste and curation beats the promise of volume.

Leans into Theory of Constraints with a twist. Constraints are Scarcity, Risk and Coordination.

**Scarcity** - something that is a key resource is limited. In the case of shipping he shows that communications with the outside world - to keep up to date on schedule or summon help in emergency. So the radio operator with Morse code was the constraint. In modern software development the constraint is often Quality Assurance or Code Review.

**Risks** - Anaesthesiologist in a surgical environment. They're managing risk in the surgery. Paying attention to the patient's vital signs. Too much anaesthetic and the patients organs will shut down. Too little and they will wake up in the midst of the surgery.

**Coordination** - Many moving parts that need to align across groups. The book's example is getting a movie made. From writing, actors, sets, costumes, cinematography, funding, editing and ... . In this world the Producer is the coordinator and the becomes the constraint.

When all wine, good, bad and awful became more widely available the value of the sommelier increased. Wine is no longer scarce. Further, the internet is full of reviews about wine and vineyards. The constraint now is knowing where to look and who to trust. The sommelier is curating and instilling confidence. A restaurant uses them now as part of a package, promising people a better dining experience.

### Don't Chase the Skill, Follow the Constraint
Up skilling is still valuable, but only in the context of understanding the constraints first. Look to where the scarcity, risk or coordination constraints are and up skill for those problems.

> Skills are only valuable in relation to solving a constraint.

The evolution of the role of radiologists is a good example. They go from interpreting scans, to providing context for their colleagues. A shadow on a lung has a different meaning depending on the history of a patient. They participate more in the discussion of how to treat a cancer. *The implied claim that AI would get better than humans at reading X-ray and other images, still hasn't panned out.*

When constraints change, the roles that had value in the old case lose value. However, new roles emerge to tackle the new constraints.

The core claim of the book thus far: AI unbundles some tasks. Work that used to be valuable is no longer valuable. Instead of scarcity of skills, the constraints will be handling risk and coordination.

**Risks** with a new technology, we look for risks within the technology itself. Example elevators, the first question is what happens if the technology fails, will the elevator fall? The bigger risks come from the downstream effects. Elevators enable tall buildings, which have new structural and fire risks.

With GenAI one of the added layers of risk is the probabilistic nature of the systems.

**Coordination** tells a story of nurse navigators, helping patients deal with the increasingly messy journey through the hospital system. They use their expertise to coordinate. In the process they reduce the stress level for the patient and shorten the hospital stay.

The AI tools made some areas/departments work faster, but they were silos. The author calls this narrow. The nurse coordinator is working broadly across the whole system.

*We get to this better place, by helping people see the whole system and not the parts.*

==We only get rewarded when the value is made visible. It's not enough to improve the system if people don't see the value created.==

*Tidbit* - As AI execution scales, handling the exceptions (i.e. mislabel bins, damaged parts) becomes a much larger and more important job. The people who do this work in a warehouse do it informally and so are rarely noticed. It shows up in care environments, the system pays people for the task, yet the biggest value is the emotional support they provide.

Part of reimagining work will require making the invisible work (value?), visible to the system.

## Ch 6 Rebundling the Organization
Real Madrid, mid 2000s, built around star players. All given autonomy, yet they produced mediocre results. They optimized for individual play and didn't have a system. Barcelona, succeeded by having a system and giving players freedom within their zone.

The more complex the system, the more specialized the parts, the more important for there to be an explicit coordination system. Real Madrid failed because they lacked a system.

Mars Climate Orbiter is another example of coordination failure. One team did their math in pound-force and the other Newtons. Each team trusted the others competence and didn't question the numbers, they were experts after all. Small errors accumulated. The navigation system believed it was in the right place. When it tried to enter orbit, it instead hit the thin atmosphere and burned up. The teams had worked in isolation.

### Reducing the Coordination Tax with AI
The author claims that AI eliminates the tax. I'm troubled because he's ignoring the possibility of hallucination and the biases that the AI will add in.

He cites NotebookLLM, good. But also Persona generation. Not so good.

Leaning very heavily into Agentic execution to scout out and book sales calls -> agents to select suppliers.

Another good example is that burden of expense reporting has gone away. An AI pulls receipts from inboxes, categorizes and then sends them to the right people for approval. *Neither the employee, nor finance are dealing with the mess of expenses. A coordination tax has been eliminated*

The AI helps us when it aids the teams/organization to manage its own coordination. It enslaves us when it tells us what to do.

When we use AI in a narrow context i.e. within a single team, the team might go faster but the coordination tax goes up. Because the team using the AI produces more stuff than the other teams can handle. *This is classic Scrum deployment problem. A scrum team might significantly outpace the rest of the organization.*

> AI tool providers increasingly sell us: That AI will revolutionize knowledge work the way industrial automation revolutionized manufacturing. But there is a problem: knowledge work isn't like factory work.

Helping different teams coordinate their work, handle dependencies, work at different speeds and for different goals. This is where we need help.

Speed is not progress; Automation is not transformation.

## Ch 7. Rebundling the Value Chain

### Building Blocks on rent
The author makes the pitch that we more and more of what we need to build a business can be rented, as a series of building of blocks.

*Not super impressed with this section, where uses Mr Beast's Burger fiasco as a good and bad example*

Renting building blocks is ok to a point, what happens to quality? In addition, I can't see how this relates to AI.

# Section 3 Competitive Advantage 
## Ch 8 The Tool Integration Trap

## Ch 10 Designing for Indecision
The chapter starts with a university example with a Dean/Principal becoming concerned about unbundling. A university degree over 4 yrs is a bundled supply of knowledge. With AI unbundling and rebuilding knowledge work, the 4yr degree program may become quaint.

The learning journey becomes fragmented, how do I and like minded people create an adaptive path (?) where we help our learners on their journey. Each with an individual learning path. How do we help them select the next micro-credential that meets employers needs?",

{
  "id": "3F5287A2-470C-4035-864A-6A2222642473",
  "title": "I'm trying to study what useful Claude skills I can find/create for Scrum Masters, Product Owners and Agile Coaches. Given what I’ve seen so far, actual Scrum Masters etc are safe.",
  "content": "I'm trying to study what useful Claude skills I can find/create for Scrum Masters, Product Owners and Agile Coaches. Given what I’ve seen so far, actual Scrum Masters etc are safe.

Apparently, Scrum Masters:
- Run Daily Standup as progress summaries
- Plan Sprints based on Capacity allocation with velocity tracking
- Run Sprint Reviews and Retrospectives where the AI replaces all human thought

content.text: The July trash items were already handled by you — I'll leave those. That leaves 4 live July items. Now the Jan/Feb batch (18 items) — reading them:

{
  "id": "11AE9528-8A8E-49F9-AE7F-C6E94D96D913",
  "title": "Your Concierge MVP idea aligns well with Ignite. If I understand correctly, you're proposing:",
  "content": "Your Concierge MVP idea aligns well with Ignite. If I understand correctly, you're proposing: 
1. You share your goal + context (helping clients thrive with GenAI)
2. I/the agent crafts action steps based on that context
3. You execute and report back what worked vs. needed tweaking

This would essentially be a manual test run of Ignite's core loop - which is valuable for me to validate before automating it. I'd love to hear more about your specific goals and pain points. Happy to hop on a call later this week if you're open to it.

Background: For the past 16 years, I've helped people learn to use Scrum, Kanban, and other Agile methods. I've focused on building teams that can deliver, quality software reliably and consistently. I've also helped people understand Product Management, in an Agile context.

For 12 of those 16 years, I've employed one person (Heather) to help me run the operations of my business. Since COVID, but especially the last 2yrs this business has been challenging. At the start of the New Year, she decided to leave the business and will transition out by the end of January. She's leaving because of the stress and instability of the business, which is entirely fair.

There are many reasons for the business problems:
- Agile went mainstream, the best people don't need my help anymore. (A good thing)
- Fake Agile - some leaders use Agile as an excuse to perpetuate their existing bad habits (i.e. micromanaging, etc) and are not interested in evolving their way of working. They give lip service to Agile but don’t want to do the hard work. (They give Agile a bad name)
- Training budgets are on hold
- Generative AI (more recently) is taking over much of the conversation in the world outside, I need to adapt to it.

I got into the Agile game in 2001, I've been one of the earlist adopters and I was an early trainer/coach. I allowed myself to ride the wave of Agile for too long. I'm at my best when I'm helping people with the new edgy stuff.

Whoa a lot of context. I already do a lot of the thinking I need below, with Claude. Ideally, I would like to follow your lead and work inside Obsidian, with access to all my years of notemaking and thinking. FWIW, aside from discussing the exit of Heather, I will happily talk about of this in public.

## The Goal
the month of January is largely focused on the question of where am I taking APR (Agile Pain Relief) from here? I want to prioritize, reading, learning and experimenting. I want to use the Hashtag BuildInPublic model to help garner feedback and direction. The topic area is likely to be AI and it's affect on Software Development/Agile/ScrumMasters/ProductOwners/ScrumTeams/ProjectManagers and I will use an Agile approach to helping people adapt to the changes.

The two main important questions for the month of January are
- What experiments should I run to test what the market wants? (Discovery Interviews and ??)
- What do I measure to determine the success of my experiments?


--

It sounds like January is a pivotal month for APR, focusing on adapting to the evolving landscape of software development, particularly with the rise of Generative AI. Your goal to prioritize reading, learning, and experimenting, while leveraging the #BuildInPublic model for feedback, is a solid approach to navigate these changes.

Let's break down your key questions for the month:

### 1. What experiments should I run to test what the market wants?

Beyond discovery interviews, here are some experiment ideas to test market interest and refine your offerings:

*   **Content Series/Webinar on AI & Agile:**
    *   **Experiment:** Host a free webinar or a short, multi-part blog/social media series titled something like "Navigating the AI Revolution: What Agile Teams Need to Know."
    *   **Goal:** Gauge interest through registrations, engagement (questions, comments), and post-event feedback. This tests demand for your insights on this specific topic.
*   **"AI-Augmented Scrum" Workshop/Masterclass:**
    *   **Experiment:** Offer a paid, short-form workshop or masterclass focusing on practical ways AI can enhance Scrum roles (e.g., AI for backlog refinement, AI for test automation, AI for retrospectives).
    *   **Goal:** Test willingness to pay for specific, actionable AI-related Agile training. Success would be filling the seats.
*   **AI Impact Assessment Tool/Quiz:**
    *   **Experiment:** Develop a simple online quiz or assessment tool (e.g., "How Ready is Your Team for AI?") that helps ScrumMasters, Product Owners, etc., understand their current standing regarding AI adoption.
    *   **Goal:** Measure lead generation (sign-ups for results), engagement, and the types of results people are most interested in. This aligns with your previous work on quizzes for Scrum effectiveness.
*   **"AI for [Specific Role]" Mini-Guide/Cheatsheet:**
    *   **Experiment:** Create a free, downloadable resource tailored to a specific role (e.g., "AI Tools for the Modern ScrumMaster").
    *   **Goal:** Test download rates and gather feedback on the usefulness of the content. This can identify which roles are most actively seeking AI solutions.
*   **"Ask Me Anything" (AMA) Sessions on AI & Agile:**
    *   **Experiment:** Schedule live AMA sessions on LinkedIn or Mastodon where you answer questions about AI's impact on Agile development.
    *   **Goal:** Measure participation, the volume and nature of questions asked, and identify recurring themes or pain points.

### 2. What do I measure to determine the success of my experiments?

To measure the success of these experiments, consider a mix of quantitative and qualitative metrics, focusing on engagement and potential customer interest:

**Primary Metrics (LinkedIn):**
*   **Reach & Impressions:** How many people saw your content related to the experiment?
*   **Engagement Rate:** Likes, comments, shares, saves on posts announcing or discussing the experiment.
*   **Click-Through Rate (CTR):** For links to webinars, workshop sign-ups, or resource downloads.
*   **Lead Generation:** Number of sign-ups for webinars, masterclasses, or downloadable content.
*   **Direct Messages/Inquiries:** The number and quality of private messages asking for more information or expressing interest.
*   **Follower Growth:** While not the primary goal, an increase in relevant followers can indicate growing interest.

**Secondary Metrics (Mastodon):**

*   **Engagement:** Boosts, replies, favourites on your posts.
*   **Follower Growth:** Similar to LinkedIn, but within the Mastodon ecosystem.
*   **Referral Traffic:** If you link to landing pages, track traffic from Mastodon.

**Qualitative Metrics:**

*   **Feedback:** Direct comments, survey responses, or messages about the value of the content or experiments.
*   **Recurring Themes:** What questions or challenges keep coming up across different experiments? This is gold for identifying market needs.
*   **Sentiment:** The overall tone of the feedback and discussions.

By running these experiments and diligently measuring their outcomes, you can gain clarity on what resonates most with your target audience and where APR can best focus its efforts in the AI-driven future of software development.",

{
  "id": "F3DFF547-5A7E-4148-B1CB-4C8D49FACF36",
  "title": "GenAI is here for good.",
  "content": "GenAI is here for good. 

Friday Feb 13th - the perfect date for this. https://agilepainrelief.com/where-is-ai-taking-software-development/

**Post 1: The Hype vs. Reality**

**LinkedIn:** GenAI is the loudest hype cycle I've ever witnessed. Trillions in GPU investments? Yes. Trillions in actual value? No evidence yet.

On Feb 13, I'm hosting a webinar that strips away the noise and focuses on what is happening--including the risks that OpenAI and Anthropic don't advertise.

Beyond the hype. Real talk about AI in software development.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic

**Mastodon/BlueSky:** GenAI is the loudest hype cycle ever. Trillions in GPU investments, but where's the actual value? Feb 13 webinar: stripping away the noise to focus on what is happening. #AIinSoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic
* * *

**Post 2: The Commodification Reality**

**LinkedIn:** Here's what GenAI is actually doing: commodifying repetitive work. The first draft is cheap. But cheap ≠ reliable, secure, or fit for purpose.

A less experienced team can produce faster with AI. The missing ingredient? Taste. The judgment to catch edge cases, security gaps, and technical debt.

The bill always comes due later.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic

**Mastodon/BlueSky:** GenAI commodifies repetitive work--the first draft is cheap. But cheap ≠ reliable or secure. The missing ingredient is taste: judgment to catch edge cases and security gaps. The bill always comes due. #AIinSoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic
* * *

**Post 3: The Speed-Up Myth**

**LinkedIn:** GenAI speeds up strategic thinking--but not magically. The speed-up depends on: • Your ability to frame the problem • Providing clear constraints • Evaluating the quality of output

Use it as a sparring partner, not a replacement for thinking.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic

**Mastodon/BlueSky:** GenAI speeds up strategic thinking--but not magically. It depends on framing problems, setting constraints, and evaluating output. Use it as a sparring partner, not a thinking replacement. #AIinSoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic
* * *

**Post 4: The Judgment Problem**

  "content": "How to deal with unavoidable on-demand tasks in Scrum?
Scrum team doesn't want to have standups; how to handle this?
What are developers expected to do during testing in the latter half of each Sprint?

Numbering Sprints across products – should they reset or continue ad infinitum?

Can we have a Sprint Zero with no deliverable code?
What is a failed sprint?
Has the Daily Scrum be held every day of the sprint?
How to estimate story points if team members work on different applications?
How to estimate amount of work/man hours for an unfamiliar task?
How to calculate velocity when using fibonacci estimates?
Do we need to update time estimates when we estimate based on story points?
What should you do with story points which aren't completed in sprint?
Should chores and technical debt be estimated or not?
How to estimate a project budget using story points?
When are Story Points and priority estimated in the planning phase?
How to handle disagreements about story-point estimates in Scrum?
Is it fine to correct an estimation of a story during execution?
How to estimate the benefit of adding a software feature?
Why are developers expected to estimate tasks at all?

{
  "id": "422F0F0C-E72E-4D10-8D8B-052D3E68F91A",
  "title": "How to deal with unavoidable on-demand tasks in Scrum?",
  "content": "How to deal with unavoidable on-demand tasks in Scrum?
Scrum team doesn't want to have standups; how to handle this?
What are developers expected to do during testing in the latter half of each Sprint?
How can we fix Sprint Planning meetings that are unproductive?
Numbering Sprints across products – should they reset or continue ad infinitum?
Is it necessary to address all three questions every day in the Scrum?
Can we have a Sprint Zero with no deliverable code?
What is a failed sprint?
Has the Daily Scrum be held every day of the sprint?
How to estimate story points if team members work on different applications?
How to estimate amount of work/man hours for an unfamiliar task?
How to calculate velocity when using fibonacci estimates?
Do we need to update time estimates when we estimate based on story points?
What should you do with story points which aren't completed in sprint?
Should chores and technical debt be estimated or not?
How to estimate a project budget using story points?
When are Story Points and priority estimated in the planning phase?
How to handle disagreements about story-point estimates in Scrum?
Is it fine to correct an estimation of a story during execution?
How to estimate the benefit of adding a software feature?
Why are developers expected to estimate tasks at all?

content.text: The Scrum-questions draft had a huge accidental console-log blob appended, but the useful part is a list of Scrum FAQ topics. Continuing through the rest:

{
  "id": "9E77577E-1211-48F3-B31A-155BA842ED3E",
  "title": "You have an ill-defined user story, and you decide to talk to GenAI to get some ideas. (My weapon of choice is Claude Code.) It sounds confident, and the ideas seem good, so you decide to go with it. Luckily, you haven't automated away QA, and they found a problem.",
  "content": "\n\nYou have an ill-defined user story, and you decide to talk to GenAI to get some ideas. (My weapon of choice is Claude Code.) It sounds confident, and the ideas seem good, so you decide to go with it. Luckily, you haven't automated away QA, and they found a problem.\n\nThe LLM is a prediction machine, it's job is to predict the next token in a sequence. It doesn’t understand the bigger picture; it just guesses what comes next based on the average of the text it was trained on. It sounded confident, but that's a side effect of their training, not a sign of intelligence.\n\nThe model doesn’t know if it should be 95% confident or 25% confident; it's just guessing, in response to your prompt. This is the problem baked into the technology itself. And it's actively misleading.\n\nWhen an LLM says something is true, we need to verify whether it’s true. That also means we should only use it in places where we understand enough to evaluate its output.\n\nWhere are you using GenAI, that you need to check the output more carefully? \n\n\n",

  "id": "8E0D8C30-217D-4BD9-85F3-79656D31A71D",
  "title": "I currently use the Circle.so to host online learning content.",
  "content": "I currently use the Circle.so to host online learning content.

Circle provides me the following functionality:
- Discussion forum
- Learning spaces for courses
- Payment gateway
- Login protection

I don't love the fact that all learning content is added by hand and there is no version control.

By comparison, I host my website using Astro + Netifly. I write my content in Markdown/MDX and then it is compiled to html on checkin/deploy.

Is a platform that is designed for someone to publish learning content via a push from a source code control system? Markdown or not.

In order of importance:
- Learning content - pushed via git
- Login system to protect content
- Discussion platform
- Payment gateway
- Quizzes and submitting homework assignments.

Learning content is text, videos, images and downloadable PDFs. Not interactive material.",

{
  "id": "2AF2CE70-2F86-46A9-B1A0-2731C3A43A44",
  "title": "Here are 20 questions from the sources that provide significant depth and detail regarding specific organisational and project challenges:",
  "content": "Here are 20 questions from the sources that provide significant depth and detail regarding specific organisational and project challenges:\n\n1. **How to manage a team split between an \"old guard\" and a \"new guard\"**: a team of developers is divided between members with 10+ years of tenure who refuse to merge code until a whole Epic is reviewed, and new members who prefer frequent merging; this causes \"merge hell\" and errors during integration.\n3. **Handling the \"Sunk Cost\" negotiation trap**: a company releases features as they are developed (continuous delivery), but the customer purposefully slows the sales process until the project is 75% done and then threatens cancellation to force a massive price discount.\n4. **Managing the \"Dead Horse\" retrospective ban**: a project is plagued by recurring impediments outside the team's control, such as a third-party supplier dragging their feet on kitchen layout samples, leading management to ban these topics from discussion in retrospectives.\n7. **Specialization within a Scrum team**: a team consists of 12 developers where everyone works on separate submodules (one-man shows), leading to code reviews where members do not have the expertise to review each other's work.\n8. **The \"Status Pull\" efficiency argument**: how to convince a manager that \"status pull\" meetings--where an entire team sits passively while one person reports status--are a form of \"waste\" even if the manager finds them \"convenient\".\n9. **The \"Tom\" problem with requirements adherence**: how to manage a senior developer who consistently delivers 80% of a task, argues that his choice of button colour (green instead of blue) is better than the wireframe, and adds unplanned features like \"login animations\".\n10. **Navigating the \"Revenue-Impacting\" bug priority**: a sales-focused coworker wants a new priority category for bugs that \"impact revenue,\" creating a situation where everything is \"crisis-urgent\" and pushes aside other revenue-generating features.\n11. **Managing \"Larry vs Winston\" working hours**: how to handle a team where one developer (\"laid-back Larry\") is stressed by an 8-hour day and needs breaks, while a \"workaholic Winston\" feels he is doing all the hard work while Larry is \"free-riding\".\n13. **The \"Single Point of Contact\" tool conflict**: how to manage a contractual \"single point of contact\" clause when using project tools like Basecamp that naturally encourage communication between many different people.\n14. **The \"Vicious Firefighting\" support cycle**: how to protect a Scrum team when developers are constantly approached by POs and support staff to fix setups or recover data, disrupting the intended Sprint Goal.\n16. **The \"Zero Sum\" KPI game**: how to align performance metrics when an engineer's KPI (passing QA with no bugs) and a tester's KPI (finding more bugs per issue) create a conflict of interest and hurt morale.\n18. **The \"Specialist\" utilization problem**: how to manage and record the time of an \"adopted expert\" (like a UX Guru) who only has 10% worth of work in a Sprint but is required to attend every standup and avoid \"outside\" interruptions.\n19. **Determining \"Project\" vs \"Process\" in maintenance**: how to define the role of a PM in a company where management wants a PM assigned to software maintenance teams as operational support, even though the work has no distinct end.\n20. **Handling \"Delayed Information\" from customers**: how to manage 60 user stories that are \"done\" from a development standpoint but cannot be closed because the team has been waiting on a unresponsive customer for information for weeks.\n\n**Summary Analogy**: Dealing with these deep project management issues is like **navigating a minefield of human nature**; you must balance the \"old guard\" versus \"new guard\" (culture), manage \"vaporware\" and \"sunk costs\" (ethics and finance), and align \"Larry\" with \"Winston\" (team harmony) while the clock of \"stifling\" regulations counts down.",

content.text:
{
  "id": "A6E83CD6-71B8-499D-8257-94D70E7D09AD",
  "title": "GenAI and it's unintended consequences.",
  "content": "GenAI and it's unintended consequences. \n\nIt's being used to create specifications for features. I know because I’ve done it myself.\n\nI've used both Qwen (locally on my laptop) and Claude Code. Both can create detailed specifications for a small feature. These can then be used to detailed unit tests. In turn I do a TDD style of approach to get the feature done.\n\nAs usual, there are unintended consequences:\n- Some of the specs are just plain wrong, it offers to build an enterprise grade solution for the first version of a feature.\n- More specs mean more test cases which means alot more time required to review them carefully\n- With the increase in test cases, there are redundant test cases and gaps in the test cases\n- Some of the test cases are technically correct, but they're testing an implementation detail rather than the feature itself.\n- Sometimes the model wants to build functions that are exist in the framework already\n- On one occasion, I was offered a regex solution to parsing finding a daily journal entry (in Obsidian). The problem is that the regex was fragile and unique to me case. There are standard approaches in Obsidian to ask for daily journal entries. So we shouldn't even be looking for filename, instead asking the system for the files themselves.\n\n(Caveat Emptor - I'm a solo developer, on this product, working in my spare time. I'm using Typescript, SvelteKit and Supabase. 6 months ago I'd never touched any of these technologies. I wouldn't have gotten as far as I have without GenAI.)",

In turn I do a TDD style of approach to get the feature done.\n\nAs usual, there are unintended consequences:\n- Some of the specs are just plain wrong, it offers to build an enterprise grade solution for the first version of a feature.\n- More specs mean more test cases which means alot more time required to review them carefully\n- With the increase in test cases, there are redundant test cases and gaps in the test cases\n- Some of the test cases are technically correct, but they're testing an implementation detail rather than the feature itself.\n- Sometimes the model wants to build functions that are exist in the framework already\n- On one occasion, I was offered a regex solution to parsing finding a daily journal entry (in Obsidian). The problem is that the regex was fragile and unique to me case. There are standard approaches in Obsidian to ask for daily journal entries. So we shouldn't even be looking for filename, instead asking the system for the files themselves.\n\n(Caveat Emptor - I'm a solo developer, on this product, working in my spare time. I'm using Typescript, SvelteKit and Supabase. 6 months ago I'd never touched any of these technologies. I wouldn't have gotten as far as I have without GenAI.)",

  "content": "Use the NICE goals a framework to help reframe my more vague quarterly goals as Nice Goals. Each section should have 1-2 NICE Goals.

Nice is a framework for setting goals that emphasizes the human element and focuses on the journey towards achieving them. Unlike the more common SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals, NICE goals prioritize aspects that can make the process more engaging and sustainable.

The NICE framework stands for:

**Near-term**: Goals that are focused on the immediate future.
**Input-based**: Goals that concentrate on the actions and steps taken, rather than solely on the outcome.
**Controllable**: Goals that are within the individual's direct influence and control.
**Energizing**: Goals that are motivating and inspiring, making the pursuit enjoyable. 

By incorporating these principles, NICE goals aim to be actionable, immediate, and within the leader's control, making goal-setting more effective and ensuring goals "actually stick." 

For example, a SMART goal might be to "Lose 20 pounds by July 1st." In contrast, a NICE goal would focus on the process: "Exercise at least 30 minutes daily, doing something fun, manageable, and sweaty." 

 This approach emphasizes the journey and the steps one can focus on to reach their desired destination

  "content": "#ClaudeCode makes small missteps. I'm trying to automate many small tasks with ClaudeCode. Today, I'm exporting data from BufferApp, which doesn't currently have an API. I got Claude to write a Typescript/Playwright program to extract the data. Following a pattern of progressive development, I started with LinkedIn -> Mastodon -> BlueSky.\n\nSince it's the same core buffer page (just with different filters), I expected a core component with handlers for the different types. What I got was three different batches of code, ~2/3s of which were the same. The CSV output of Mastodon is in a different order than the others. Finally, Claude decided to run the Mastodon version directly in its own chat window, rather than leaving the work to the human allegedly in the loop. Claude burned through my morning's supply of tokens (I'm only on the Pro Plan), with that mess.\n\nIn the long run, the code quality for this task isn't important. It will work for the next few months, until Buffer releases their API. In addition, this frees me up to do the deeper analysis.\n\n#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic \n\n",

  "title": "I was recently trying to download all my social media analytics from Buffer, and I noticed a common pattern in the use of  Claude and Playwright: 'Most people suggestions were to get Claude to drive Playwright'.",
  "content": "I was recently trying to download all my social media analytics from Buffer, and I noticed a common pattern in the use of  Claude and Playwright: 'Most people suggestions were to get Claude to drive Playwright'.\nThis was not in the least bit tempting, however it led me to a realization about the real cost of AI automation.\n\nIf I give an AI a repeatable task, then everytime it runs I need to check the results carefully. There is an ongoing \"cognitive tax\" to be paid.\n\nInstead if I get the AI to write the code to do the actual work, I work harder upfront. However, in the long run I can safely run the task each time without having to carefully check the results. In addition if fails eventually the failure will be self evident - no output or completely incorrect data. For bonus points, the second approach is also more efficient in terms of LLM tokens and electricity use.\n\nWhat decisions are you making to reduce the Cognitive Tax?\n\n#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #BuildInPublic \n\n",

  "id": "AF90D1DF-BEE6-48B6-B14E-326FBBCB8F78",
  "title": "Agile practitioners are currently navigating a profound structural and philosophical transition, shifting from manual facilitators to "orchestrators" who use AI to manage administrative "grunt work" while simultaneously facing existential fears regarding job devaluation and the rise of "management-b…",
  "content": "Agile practitioners are currently navigating a profound structural and philosophical transition, shifting from manual facilitators to "orchestrators" who use AI to manage administrative "grunt work" while simultaneously facing existential fears regarding job devaluation and the rise of "management-by-dashboard".

### **Emotional Responses**

The emotional climate within the Agile community is a complex tapestry of conflicting sentiments triggered by rapid technological shifts:

- **Hope:** Practitioners feel a sense of relief at the prospect of **"cognitive decoupling"**, where AI handles administrative "grunt work" like ticket formatting and retrospective synthesis. They hope this allows a return to core human coaching, such as fostering high-performance team dynamics.
- **Fear:** This is primarily triggered by **"Reductions in Force" (RIFs)** and organizational restructuring where "Agile Coach" roles are targeted for elimination. There is anxiety about the **"Great Hiring Implosion,"** where machines are perceived to hire other machines, alienating humans from the talent lifecycle.
- **Anger:** Many are infuriated by **"Agile Theater Chaos,"** where AI is used to mask managerial incompetence or generate hollow, professional-sounding communications that lack genuine Agile commitment.
- **Excitement:** There is a sense of "weird fantasy" among those achieving **"10x" productivity gains**, using tools to build in minutes what previously took an entire sprint.
- **Resignation:** Some have accepted that AI adoption is **inevitable** and are focusing on survival and reskilling, believing AI will eventually "hack the operating system of human civilization".

### **Current Context**

The modern practitioner's environment has shifted from manual ceremony animation to high-level orchestration:

- **Current Tools:**
    - **Specialised Agents:** Tools like **Telos** and **Vomoai** are used to consolidate notes from Slack, emails, and calls to draft Jira tickets.
    - **Custom GPTs:** The **"Retrospective Insights Analyst"** GPT processes raw data from Miro boards to identify friction points human facilitators might miss.
    - **Transcription Engines:** Used to automate sprint transcriptions and summarize user research.
    - **Morale Tools:** Some use **Suno AI** to generate "Pep Songs" for teams during difficult sprint demos.
- **Typical Workday:** Practitioners spend their mornings on **"Morning Orchestration,"** reviewing AI summaries of asynchronous stand-ups and code commits to find blockers. This is followed by AI-assisted backlog refinement and strategic "entrepreneurial" tasks, such as testing business hypotheses.
- **Current Goals:** The primary goal is to **scale coaching** across 3--4 teams simultaneously by offloading "synthesis grunt work" to AI.

### **Specific Pain Points**

Practitioners have documented concrete failures where AI implementation met operational reality:

- **Copy-Paste Fatigue:** A major frustration is the disjointed hand-off between AI chat interfaces and systems of record like Jira, which one practitioner found so **"impractical"** that writing tickets manually remained faster.
- **Literalness and Lack of Intuition:** AI coding assistants are "terrible at reading minds"; if a requirement is vague, the AI "goes off the rails".
- **"Vanilla" Personas:** In user-centered design, AI-generated personas often lack **"illegible" social and political nuances**, resulting in over-sanitized, unrealistic representations that miss core user problems.
- **Adaptations:**
    - **"Waterfall 2.0":** To compensate for AI's literalness, teams are spending **three times more time** on upfront design and writing 5-page specifications that read like legal contracts.
    - **Micro-Waterfalls:** Some teams run "small waterfall" cycles where they write a spec, have AI build it in minutes, and immediately validate it, maintaining Agile's release cadence while adding Waterfall's rigor.
    - **"Vibe-Coding":** Using AI for exploratory, rapid brainstorming before switching to strict "Spec" mode for execution.

### **Ideal Scenarios**

Practitioners use "magic wand" thinking to envision a future where AI serves as a guardian of team health:

- **Burnout Sentinel:** A wish for AI that can identify organizational issues like **burnout** or stress signals in communication patterns before they manifest as failures.
- **Real-time Behavioral Feedback:** An "AI Coach" that provides immediate feedback during meetings, pointing out an **"uneven distribution of speech"** or suggesting more open-ended questions.
- **Ultra-efficient Units:** A bold vision for teams to shrink into high-performing units of just **"2 people plus an AI"**that build products at the speed of thought.
- **What they hope WON'T happen:**
    - AI becoming a **"Machiavellian prince"** used by leadership to enforce bureaucratic control or eliminate "human sense-making".
    - A total **loss of essential human skills** and a "mediocrity" caused by overreliance on technology that makes teams fragile.


Drawing on the provided sources, the following perspectives represent the diverse roles navigating the intersection of Agile and AI. These details are structured to support the creation of realistic personas for customer discovery.

### **1. The "Entrepreneurial" Strategist**

This perspective views AI as a "superpower" for those who move beyond administrative tasks to focus on high-stakes business hypotheses.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** CTO, Product Lead, or "Agile Alchemist".
- **Demographics:** Large-scale public sector (e.g. NHS England), government AI incubators, or high-growth tech startups. Often high-level experience (CTO-level).
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Aims to achieve **"10x" impact** with small, high-functioning teams (fewer than 7 people). Needs tools for **"Morning Orchestration"** to review asynchronous stand-ups and code commits.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Hates "meeting entropy" and the "busywork singularity" where AI generates summaries of summaries. Fears that "hybrid work" is becoming an obsolete concept replaced by "blended work" where human agency is redistributed.
- **Work Environment:** Fast-flowing information environments (Slack, Teams, GitHub) where the goal is to "dance with" rather than master a colossal system.
- **Real Story/Quote:** One CTO noted that while AI can give you "a million prototypes," the real bottleneck is getting feedback: *"Artefacts are not really what we're here for... we are demonstrably optimising about a mile from the bottleneck"*.
* * *

### **2. The Overwhelmed "Scribe" (Backlog Manager)**

This role is currently the most vulnerable to AI displacement as their primary value--documentation and coordination--is easily automated.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** Product Owner (PO), Junior Project Manager, or "Backlog Clerk".
- **Demographics:** Mid-to-large corporations; often has a "light CS background" (e.g. VBA/SQL) but is not a primary developer.
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Needs to consolidate "scattered context" from Slack, emails, and customer calls into Jira tickets without manual copy-pasting.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** **"Copy-paste fatigue"**--finding that moving text between AI and Jira is so friction-heavy that manual writing is faster. Fears the **"Great Hiring Implosion"** where machines hire machines, making their facilitation skills redundant.
- **Work Environment:** A "feature factory" where the focus is on specification over value.
- **Real Story/Quote:** A PO frustrated by scattered data asked: *"I spend a stupid amount of time writing tickets... not because the writing is hard, but because the context is scattered everywhere... Is everyone still doing this manually?"*.
* * *

### **3. The "Structuralist" Purist**

This perspective rejects AI for administrative tasks, arguing that if a Scrum Master is busy updating tickets, the system design is broken.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** Senior Agile Coach, Scrum Master, or "Friction Fixer".
- **Demographics:** 20+ years of experience; high-income countries (Finland, USA, UK); often technical veterans.
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Aims for **"Cognitive Decoupling"**--using AI only if it handles "synthesis grunt work" to allow a return to human coaching.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Infuriated by **"Agile Theater"** and the "Agile Industrial Complex". Fears AI will become a "Machiavellian prince" used by leadership to enforce bureaucratic control.
- **Work Environment:** Values "face-to-face conversation" and physical index cards over digital boards.
- **Real Story/Quote:** A veteran coach stated: *"I don't recognize Agile any more... the focus has shifted from developers to executives, mostly because executives can pay those sweet, sweet consulting contracts"*.
* * *

### **4. The "Technical Veteran" Coach**

A practitioner who insists that Agile coaching is ineffective without deep technical domain knowledge.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** Release Train Engineer (RTE) or Scrum Master with a former Software Engineering background.
- **Demographics:** 35+ years in software; often age 60+; works in highly technical industries like Automotive or Telecomm.
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Needs to demonstrate **"Technical Competence"**--being able to walk the walk, like demonstrating a unit test or CI technique.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Frustrated by Scrum Masters who measure themselves by "how many LEGO games they know" rather than understanding engineering blockers.
- **Work Environment:** Scaled Agile environments (SAFe) where they must eliminate dependencies to stay small.
- **Real Story/Quote:** One practitioner noted that AI coding assistants are mind-blind: *"If your requirements are vague, the AI goes off the rails... we are spending three times more time on upfront design and specifications"*.
* * *

### **5. The "Fuming" Executive**

A leadership perspective focused on ROI, often disillusioned with the speed of traditional Agile transformations.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** CEO, CFO, or "Operating Model Expert".
- **Demographics:** Large corporations or government agencies.
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Needs **"Management-by-Dashboard"** and clear metrics to justify the cost of Agile to stockholders.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Frustrated by "conflicting priorities" among Agile leads that do not add up to strategic goals. Afraid that Agile is "not working for us" and seeks to "check the box" for transformation by the end of the year.
- **Work Environment:** The "Executive Board Room," often isolated from the "@GEMBA" (actual work floor).
- **Real Story/Quote:** A CEO in an Agile Theater scenario was described as *"fuming"* because *"None of the local priorities... add up to his own strategic priorities"*.
* * *

### **6. The User Research (UR) Specialist**

Focuses on capturing authentic user needs and is highly critical of AI's tendency to over-simplify human behavior.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** UX Researcher, Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Expert, or Persona Scientist.
- **Demographics:** Academic or specialized industry research roles; diverse international backgrounds (Finland, South Korea, Lebanon).
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Needs to avoid **"Algorithmic Othering"** where minority identities are rendered hypervisible but inauthentic. Aims for "Human-Centered AI" (HCAI) protocols.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Frustrated by **"Over-sanitization"**--AI omitting realistic negative traits or challenges to produce "unrealistically positive" user archetypes. Fears AI "hallucinations" where plausible-sounding user data has no basis in actual research.
- **Work Environment:** Laboratory or digital design settings focused on data-driven personas (DDPs).
- **Real Story/Quote:** A researcher found that in addiction studies, AI mixed up symptoms of different drugs: *"The personas consistently portrayed addiction narratives in an unrealistically positive light, minimizing the severity of substance abuse issues"*.

{
  "id": "3E5A84BC-DC24-4E73-BE97-7CEFAC51E638",
  "title": "BDD notes",
  "content": "BDD notes

- One paper was around testing UI PostHoc - well done and not useful.
See Panda Post
- Has anyone written a good BDD discovery coach. Could I turn the example mapping blog post into a discovery tool?
- Automating creation of Playwright tests and also **interpreting results**
- BDD collaboration - most important in cases of: complexity; Regulatory; Legacy

Current generation reasoning relies on statistical pattern matching. Reasoning responses are often just replicating patterns seen in training data. This is not a logical deduction.

Code and architectural quality in general, Models suffer in their attempts to create good quality code:
- trained on a mass of code across the internet -> No coherent principles involved
- training data isn't grounded in OO, Functional Programming or any other principles -> can be added by use "skills" et al however this is a context consuming band-aid
- May follow unconventional patterns making it harder to understand
- Doesn't know the problem domain it's being asked to work in.
- Doesn't have access to all of the relevant data. Code, User Stories, etc and not all stored in the same place. In addition they're often not written in the same language 
- Context windows are still a problem - even models with large context windows often 'forget' to pay attention to the bits in the middle

10 yrs ago, we all knew not to blindly paste StackOverflow code into our products. Now we do that every day and call it productivity.

  "id": "F137C90A-BCFC-421A-9D0F-4C2D92A30156",
  "title": "With some recent changes in my business, I needed a clear picture of my business: website traffic (PostHog), search rankings (Google Search Console), newsletter performance (Drip), and social media (Buffer). Several of these platforms don’t make data export easy, so I used Claude Code to write scrip…",
  "content": "With some recent changes in my business, I needed a clear picture of my business: website traffic (PostHog), search rankings (Google Search Console), newsletter performance (Drip), and social media (Buffer). Several of these platforms don’t make data export easy, so I used Claude Code to write scripts that scrape and export what I needed. This kind of thing is becoming approachable even for non-technical people. The LLM writes the code, you just run it. A useful side effect: those scripts now run on their own without any AI involvement.\n\nOnce I had the data, I had Claude analyze it alongside my business notes to produce a strategic overview and help me think through future directions. It covered an enormous amount of ground quickly. Most of the analysis was solid; where it was wrong, it wasn’t hard to correct. On my own, this would have taken most of a week.\n\nWhat surprised me was how exhausting it was. A full day of AI-assisted strategic thinking left me more drained than a normal workday. Critical thinking at that intensity and volume is tiring, even with AI doing the heavy lifting on synthesis.\n\nOne unexpected outcome: while automating some tasks in Drip, I realized how much of their API is missing functionality I need, forcing workarounds with Playwright. Combined with cost and data sovereignty concerns, it’s increasingly the wrong tool for my needs. What struck me was how quickly Gemini surfaced better alternatives, a search that would have taken me hours took minutes. LLMs are making platform switching far less intimidating.\n\nSo it helped me do my strategic thinking faster and it will save me money when I dump drip this summer.",

  "id": "E0ABC1A8-E83A-43BB-B134-DF487CD5EF11",
  "title": "Thoughtworks the Future of Software Engineering",
  "content": "\nThoughtworks the Future of Software Engineering\n\nhttps://readwise-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/media/wisereads/articles/the-future-of-software-enginee/1144.pdf\n\n## Rigour\nClearer specifications mean that User Stories will probably go away. Spending more time reviewing the specification becomes important.\n\nThe key question is what are people writing in terms of Spec-Driven Development\n\nWith TDD the agent avoids writing tests for broken code because the tests were written first. -> This implies we should spend more time reviewing the test cases to see if they're good. *Failure mode, the agent writes code and then writes tests. The tests might verify broken code.*\n\nStrongly typed, memory safe programming languages for the win. The more safety is built into the language and environment, the less work we have in the review process.\n\n**Code Review** all with the limited value of code review for quality improvement, it has also served as a mentoring model and a way to build a shared understanding of the system. What do we to offset the losses here.\n\nYet again we see a comment on these tools amplify the dysfunction in the system. Lack of decision making?",
