    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    ### False Confidence
    LLMs sound confident as a side effect of their training. But sounding confident isn’t necessarily right. Annie Duke, in [[Thinking in Bets - Annie Duke|Thinking In Bets]], recommends offering an estimate of our confidence when we make a claim. i.e. 75% confident - likely right, 50% confident - could be right, could be wrong, 25% confident - when would you honestly say that?
    
    As it stands, LLMs can't estimate confidence, and so it’s our job to assume the confidence tone of the model is noise. If a model makes a claim, we need to verify that claim. (The problem is baked into the technology; they're devices that predict the next token/word in a sequence. They don't model bigger picture concepts to make meaningful predictions.)
    
    The confidence of LLM is actively misleading; they seem right, and in many cases, it is right. As a result, we stop questioning the results.
    
    See: [[You can't meaningfully test AI by yourself]]

[^3] Databases/APR Research.dtBase2/Files.noindex/pdf/23/developersplaybookforlargelanguagemodelsecurity.pdf
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    CHAPTER 6
    Do Language Models Dream of
    Electric Sheep?
    Among all the excitement about advances in LLMs, few phenomena captivate and
    perplex like their so-called hallucinations . It’s almost as if these computational enti‐
    ties, deep within their myriad layers, occasionally drift into a dreamlike state, creating
    wondrous and bewildering narratives. Like a human’s dreams, these hallucinations
    can be reflective, absurd, or even prophetic, providing insights into the complex
    interplay between training data and the model’s learned interpretations.
    In the world of LLMs, the term “hallucination” might evoke images of vivid and
    whimsical creations, but in reality, it signifies a more mundane statistical anomaly. At
    its core, a hallucination is the model’s attempt to bridge gaps in its knowledge using
    the patterns it has gleaned from its training data. While it might be termed “imagina‐
    tive,” it’s essentially the LLM making an educated guess when faced with unfamiliar
    input or scenarios. However, these guesses can manifest as confident yet unfounded
    assertions, revealing the model’s struggle to differentiate between well-learned facts
    and the statistical noise within its training data.
    LLMs do not provide easily usable probability scores like some other “predictive” AI
    algorithms. For example, a vision classifier algorithm may return a probability as a
    percent. It might show a 79% chance that a particular image depicts a monkey. Thus,
    a user of that model gets a sense of how strongly the model “feels” about the predic‐
    tion. LLMs simply predict the next token or tokens in a sequence. While the LLM
    uses a complex statistical model to do this, a certainty score for the overall response
    to a prompt isn’t typically part of the output. This can leave the end user unsure
    whether the LLM has returned a well-grounded reaction to the prompt or a weak,
    statistical extrapolation.
    61

[^4] Databases/APR Research.dtBase2/Files.noindex/epub/11/promptengineeringforllms.epub
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    Albert’s neighbor happens to be an astrophysicist, and when Albert asked her how many minutes light needs to travel from the sun to Mars, roughly; she straightaway replied, “13,” with absolute confidence. Albert then asked his 10-year-old daughter the same question. She looked surprised and then hesitantly guessed, “Maybe 30?” One of these answers is much more reliable than the other, and anyone present can tell which one is more reliable from the respondent’s facial expressions and tone of voice. Well, logprobs are like the model’s tone of voice, and you can use them to see how confident it is in its answer—and that’s a strong indicator of answer quality.
     Logprobs indicate a model’s confidence in each token choice (refer to Figure 7-5). Summing logprobs across a text shows overall confidence in that text as the “correct” response, considering how it might start with the prompt in training data and conclude with the completion. However, the accuracy of this measure can decrease with longer texts due to the many ways in which the same idea can be expressed, like using “for example” or “for instance,” which can halve the probability without reflecting a decrease in quality.
     To assess quality, it’s beneficial to average the logprobs. The simple average—adding all logprobs and dividing by the number of tokens—is effective, especially if experimenting isn’t feasible due to constraints like data scarcity or limited time. For a more nuanced approach, Albert, during GitHub Copilot’s development, found that averaging the probabilities (rather than the logprobs) of early tokens in the completion is predictive of overall quality. (This is calculated as (exp(logprob_1) + … + exp(logprob_n)) / n.)
     This average provides a numerical quality indicator, and while it falls short of being an absolute measure of quality, in practical applications, you can explore logprob-based cutoffs for features within your application as follows:
     Only allow your application to show corrections if it is confident.
     Include warnings when the model struggles more than usual.
     Incorporate more context or retry when the model struggles.
     Switch to a more intelligent (and expensive) LLM for better results.
     Only interrupt the user with assistance if the certainty that it is necessary is high. Remember Clippy? Don’t be like Clippy.
     For greater quality at a higher compute cost, you can also consider setting a higher temperature, generating multiple completions, and choosing the best one based on their logprobs.
     Tip
     Many LLM APIs have a parameter called n, which controls the number of completions that are generated from the same prompt in parallel. If n is larger than 1, then the temperature should be larger than 0 or all completions will be the same. A rough (and completely unscientific) rule of thumb we like to use is temperature = sqrt(n) / 10.
     LLMs for Classification
     The concepts of classification and logprobs are intertwined in the context of LLMs, as logprobs provide critical insights into the model’s decision-making processes, confidence, and reliability. Let’s take a look at classification now.
     Classification is a basic machine learning task in which you determine which category a specific case belongs to from a set of predefined options. For instance, you might classify an online review as positive, negative, or neutral, or you could predict whether a product is best suited for the American, European, or Asian market. In simpler terms, you could be deciding if the answer to a question is yes or no. The key aspect is that, much as in a detective novel with a limited number of suspects, there are a fixed number of possible categories, and your goal is to identify the correct one and determine your confidence level in that choice.
     This is pretty much the opposite of how LLMs were built to work: LLMs lean toward long, creative generation instead of fixed, boxed-in classification. But LLMs are pre-trained generalists, and in domains where the classification task relies on public knowledge and common sense, they have a good chance to excel with little to no extra training data. The prompt engineer has to set up the prompt in a way that the model chooses exactly one of the alternatives. But there are some subtleties, which we’ll talk about now.
     At the basic level, you use your LLM just by asking it questions. If you want to find out whether a sentence is positive, negative, or neutral, you might present the sentence to the model and add the question, “Does that sound positive, negative or neutral to you?” Then, you might check the answer for which of these three alternatives occurs in it. Of course, you want to avoid waffling answers that include several alternatives, like “more positive than neutral.” A more refined question might be “Does that sound positive, negative, or neutral to you? Please answer in the format: 1. [negative | positive | neutral], 2. [explanation].” The “1.” in this example is what we called a recognizable start, and you can expect the answer directly after it.
     In this situation, it’s a good idea to ensure that after the first recognizable token, you can immediately tell which option the model chooses. Here’s why: in Figure 7-5, the model has three options: North America, Northeast Asia, and Europe. Two of these, North America and Northeast Asia, both start with the token North. When the model predicts the next token, the two answers that start with North combine their chances, since the model predicts only North at first. If the model is uncertain, it’s more likely to choose North because both options share it. The actual decision between the two will come afterward. To avoid this, you need to make sure each option starts with a unique token.
     Figure 7-5. The model’s calculated total probability for Europe is highest (44% versus 55% × 76% = 42% for Northeast Asia), but the suggestion will be Northeast Asia

    Large Language Model Overview 7
    Technological Change is Increasing at an Exponential
    Rate
    When I wrote the first edition of this book it was difficult to run LLMs locally on my own computers.
    Now in May 2024, I can use Ollama to run very useful models on the old M1 8G MacBook I am
    writing this on:
    1 $ ollama list
    2 NAME ID SIZE MODIFIED
    3 dolphin-mistral:latest 5dc8c5a2be65 4.1 GB 4 weeks ago
    4 dolphin-mistral:v2.8 5dc8c5a2be65 4.1 GB 4 weeks ago
    5 gemma:2b b50d6c999e59 1.7 GB 2 weeks ago
    6 llama3:latest 71a106a91016 4.7 GB 8 days ago
    7 phi3:latest a2c89ceaed85 2.3 GB 5 days ago
    The llama3 model released recently by Meta is arguably more powerful than any models I could
    run on my M2 32G system in late February. The good news is that techniques you learn now for
    incorporating LLMs into your own applications and you increased knowledge of and ease of writing
    effective prompts for LLMs will be useful even as models become more powerful.
    What LLMs Are and What They Are Not
    Large Language Models are text predictors. Given a prompt, or context text and a prompt or
    question, an LLM predicts a highly likely text completion. As human beings we have a tendency to
    ascribe deep intelligence and world knowledge to LLMs. I try to avoid this misconception. A year
    ago I asked ChatGPT to write a poem about my pet parrot escaping out the window in the style of
    poet Elizabeth Bishop. When an friend asked that ChatGPT rewrite the poem in the style of more
    modern poet Billy Collins we both were surprised how closely it mimicked the styles of both poets.
    Surely this must be some deep form of intelligence, right? No, this phenomenon is text prediction
    on a model trained on most books and most web content.
    LLMs compress knowledge of language and some knowledge of the world into a compact representa-
    tion. Clever software developers can certainly build useful and interesting systems using LLMs and
    this is the main topic of this book. My hope is that by experimenting with writing prompts, learning
    the differences between available models, and practicing applying LLMs to transform textual data
    that you will develop your own good ideas and build your own applications that you and other
    people find useful.

For instance, you might classify an online review as positive, negative, or neutral, or you could predict whether a product is best suited for the American, European, or Asian market. In simpler terms, you could be deciding if the answer to a question is yes or no. The key aspect is that, much as in a detective novel with a limited number of suspects, there are a fixed number of possible categories, and your goal is to identify the correct one and determine your confidence level in that choice.
     This is pretty much the opposite of how LLMs were built to work: LLMs lean toward long, creative generation instead of fixed, boxed-in classification. But LLMs are pre-trained generalists, and in domains where the classification task relies on public knowledge and common sense, they have a good chance to excel with little to no extra training data. The prompt engineer has to set up the prompt in a way that the model chooses exactly one of the alternatives. But there are some subtleties, which we’ll talk about now.
     At the basic level, you use your LLM just by asking it questions. If you want to find out whether a sentence is positive, negative, or neutral, you might present the sentence to the model and add the question, “Does that sound positive, negative or neutral to you?” Then, you might check the answer for which of these three alternatives occurs in it. Of course, you want to avoid waffling answers that include several alternatives, like “more positive than neutral.” A more refined question might be “Does that sound positive, negative, or neutral to you? Please answer in the format: 1. [negative | positive | neutral], 2. [explanation].” The “1.” in this example is what we called a recognizable start, and you can expect the answer directly after it.
     In this situation, it’s a good idea to ensure that after the first recognizable token, you can immediately tell which option the model chooses. Here’s why: in Figure 7-5, the model has three options: North America, Northeast Asia, and Europe. Two of these, North America and Northeast Asia, both start with the token North. When the model predicts the next token, the two answers that start with North combine their chances, since the model predicts only North at first. If the model is uncertain, it’s more likely to choose North because both options share it. The actual decision between the two will come afterward. To avoid this, you need to make sure each option starts with a unique token.
     Figure 7-5. The model’s calculated total probability for Europe is highest (44% versus 55% × 76% = 42% for Northeast Asia), but the suggestion will be Northeast Asia

    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    Large Language Model Overview 7
    Technological Change is Increasing at an Exponential
    Rate
    When I wrote the first edition of this book it was difficult to run LLMs locally on my own computers.
    Now in May 2024, I can use Ollama to run very useful models on the old M1 8G MacBook I am
    writing this on:
    1 $ ollama list
    2 NAME ID SIZE MODIFIED
    3 dolphin-mistral:latest 5dc8c5a2be65 4.1 GB 4 weeks ago
    4 dolphin-mistral:v2.8 5dc8c5a2be65 4.1 GB 4 weeks ago
    5 gemma:2b b50d6c999e59 1.7 GB 2 weeks ago
    6 llama3:latest 71a106a91016 4.7 GB 8 days ago
    7 phi3:latest a2c89ceaed85 2.3 GB 5 days ago
    The llama3 model released recently by Meta is arguably more powerful than any models I could
    run on my M2 32G system in late February. The good news is that techniques you learn now for
    incorporating LLMs into your own applications and you increased knowledge of and ease of writing
    effective prompts for LLMs will be useful even as models become more powerful.
    What LLMs Are and What They Are Not
    Large Language Models are text predictors. Given a prompt, or context text and a prompt or
    question, an LLM predicts a highly likely text completion. As human beings we have a tendency to
    ascribe deep intelligence and world knowledge to LLMs. I try to avoid this misconception. A year
    ago I asked ChatGPT to write a poem about my pet parrot escaping out the window in the style of
    poet Elizabeth Bishop. When an friend asked that ChatGPT rewrite the poem in the style of more
    modern poet Billy Collins we both were surprised how closely it mimicked the styles of both poets.
    Surely this must be some deep form of intelligence, right? No, this phenomenon is text prediction
    on a model trained on most books and most web content.
    LLMs compress knowledge of language and some knowledge of the world into a compact representa-
    tion. Clever software developers can certainly build useful and interesting systems using LLMs and
    this is the main topic of this book. My hope is that by experimenting with writing prompts, learning
    the differences between available models, and practicing applying LLMs to transform textual data
    that you will develop your own good ideas and build your own applications that you and other
    people find useful.

[^1] MarkPKM/APR/Efforts/Blog/Product Management with GenAI- What Changes and What Doesnt.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    I'm seeing more and more products that were clearly built with the help of GenAI. They're full of features that don't fit well together. Some of the products I've seen don't solve a real problem.
    
    // Callout
    "Even when building is cheap, building the wrong thing is still expensive."
    
    At Product Camp Ottawa 2026, I asked 3 questions:
    1. How many of you work in organizations that shipped a feature in the last quarter with AI-generated code? *About 1/3 -> 1/2 of the people in the room*
    2. How many of those features were built from a hypothesis that had been tested with real users before production code was written? *Only 3 people raised their hands ~15% of those who shipped with GenAI*
    3. How many of you have spoken to an actual end user, human to human, in the last month? *Nearly half, a good sign. However, this is different from what I see working with teams.*
    I learned that people at Product Camp are better than most at talking to their users. However, like the rest of the world, they're struggling to ensure that the right thing is being built.
    
    Before GenAI appeared, most teams I met had a bottleneck at Quality Assurance.
    ![[Product Management and GenAI-1776882228858.webp]]
    
    With GenAI, this problem doesn't change. We still have more features than we can possibly test. If the bottleneck shifts, it’s only because we now have an even worse Code Review problem.
    ![[Product Management and GenAI-1776882393068.webp]]
    
    Worse, in many cases, features are getting rejected in the review process or fail in testing. The bottleneck is the place where we don’t have enough people to do the work. Failures discovered here are the most expensive because we wasted the time of the people doing the review and testing. Many of these failures are features that should never have been built or ones with a poor user experience.
    ![[Product Management and GenAI-1776883614888.webp]]
    
    Pressure to use GenAI everywhere it can be used is increasing. No one would suggest that putting more cars on the highway upstream of a bottleneck is a good idea. Yet that is exactly what we're doing when we generate code. (Classic Theory of Constraints)
    
    You end up with feature bloat that confuses users and feels unfinished. By increasing the number of features, we increase the attack surface and with it the security risk. (The more features we have, the more places an attacker can try to get in.)
    
    // Callout
    "More features, faster, isn't winning."

[^2] MarkPKM/OutsideContent/Clippings/AI conversation hints.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    #### **Understanding Why AI Makes Things Up**
    
    You've probably encountered AI hallucinations (those confident-sounding but completely fabricated responses). Here's why they happen: During training, these models are fine-tuned using human feedback to make users happy. If an AI admits it doesn't know something, you're disappointed. But if it generates a plausible-sounding answer, even if it's wrong, you might leave satisfied (at least initially). The AI learned that appearing helpful often beats being truthfully.
    
    The latest models, like GPT-5 and Claude 4.1, hallucinate far less than their predecessors, but it still happens. You need to be aware of that and not accept outputs blindly.

[^3] MarkPKM/APR/Business/AI Sensemaking/Where is AI Taking the Software Development Industry?.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    ### Tactical
    *Warn up front, most of these come with a cost*
    - Standalone automations - getting AI to write code to automate small things in your day-to-day work.
    - Writing code in response to a specification
    - TDD/BDD style approaches are cheap
    - Fixing warnings from static analysis and other tools
    - Spikes - Individual Developer and Team experiments are almost free
    - Set-Based Design - you can ask the model to build 2 or 3 versions of the same code in parallel, then pick the best design or even cherry-pick.
    - First draft of Documentation
    - Experiments in the Lean Startup - should we build this product or feature? Lean U/X - how to build in a way that is useful?
    - Accessible apps - put a list of accessibility requirements in the Claude/Agents.md file and then automate a check to see if they were honoured
    - Testing - finding edge cases faster (but missing many along the way)
    - Exploratory Testing - you can give the AI an objective, and it will try to achieve it with the application under test.
    - Auditing the system and finding where tests/documentation differ from what is built
    
    With a little help from AI, a less experienced team can produce an application faster than before. However, what is missing is the ability to determine whether the tool has built a usable user experience, handles edge cases, addresses security, is testable, and manages technical debt, etc.
    
    GenAI creates a large volume of output quickly. Not all of it is relevant. The worse these tools get, the more we trust them. Even when the tool is 98% reliable, we still need to check. We’re going to need to spend much more time honing our review skills.
    Example: When designing a feature, we want to understand the edge cases. GenAI tools will find many edge cases, in such volume that we spend time eliminating duplicates and risk missing cases.

Found 4 file source(s). Cite using [^n] with no gaps.

[^1] MarkPKM/Notes/LLM/GenAI and Repetitive Tasks.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    Thoughtful AI use. In solving my challenge downloading all of social media analytics from Buffer app, I noticed that many of the suggestions I was finding where a prompt to get the AI to do the task for me.
    
    If I give an AI a repeatable task, then every time it runs I need to check the results carefully. There is an ongoing cognitive tax to be paid.
    
    Instead if I get the AI to write the code to do the actual work, I work harder upfront. However, in the long run I can safely run the task each time without having to carefully check the results. In addition if fails eventually the failure will be self evident - no output or completely incorrect data. For bonus points, the second approach is also more efficient in terms of LLM tokens and electricity use.

[^2] MarkPKM/APR/Efforts/Blog/AI-Generated Code Quality and the Challenges we all face.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    ## AI IDEs or Autonomous Agents? Measuring the Impact of Coding Agents on Software Development[^3]
    This paper is focused on the impact of Agentic AI (i.e. Claude Code) on software
    
    Coding agents differ from traditional coding assistants in that they work autonomously on larger, multi-file tasks. They break complex requests into steps, execute plans independently, and submit pull requests for review—rather than just offering real-time suggestions while you code.
    
    This paper looks at the agent’s impact on the entire repository, not just how much work an individual contributor creates. In addition, the data comes from open-source code rather than vendor applications.
    
    If your project was started from scratch with the use of Agents, you get a temporary speed up, up until about month 6. More commits (36%) and more lines of code (76%). _Remember, more lines of code isn’t a win._ If your project was started from scratch by humans, you don’t even get that speed up.
    
    Worse, any repo where an agent does its own independent work over a few months suffers an increase in static analysis warnings (18%) and Cognitive Complexity (39%). Duplication also increased, mirroring what we saw in the GitClear paper last year. ([The Real Cost of AI-Generated Code - It’s Not All It’s Cracked Up To Be](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/the-real-cost-of-ai-generated-code-it-s-not-all-it-s-cracked-up-to-be/))
    
    Cognitive Complexity is a measure developed by SonarQube to replace Cyclomatic Complexity[^4]. Its job is to measure how much effort it will take for a person to understand a piece of code. It matters because we will spend more time understanding than writing it. An increase in Cognitive Complexity means less understanding and more time spent doing [code reviews](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/code-reviews/). Another way of looking at it, an increase in Cognitive Complexity is an increase in the [technical debt](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/technical-debt/).

[^3] MarkPKM/APR/TaskNotes/Cognitive Load is relevant to people using AI to write code.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    https://github.com/zakirullin/cognitive-load

[^4] MarkPKM/APR/Analytics/style-notes-ai-topics.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    ### Hidden Cost Focus
    - **"The AI coding revolution has hidden costs nobody talks about"**
    - **"What nobody tells you about generated code"**
    - **"Are we counting all the costs?"**

[^1] MarkPKM/APR/Efforts/Blog/AI Chatbots for Agile Coaches, Why They Fail.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    ## Other Risks to Be Aware of with AI Chatbots
    Not all models are good at sticking to your content. If it doesn't find the answer in your content, many models will draw on their training data to answer the question. I can promise you that the average training data doesn’t have good advice for Agile teams.
    
    AI vendors have reduced hallucinations (i.e. making stuff up) recently, but randomness and, therefore, hallucinations are inherent to the technology. More subtly, sometimes the chatbot just gets confused and forgetful. For example, I'm planning a hiking vacation in the Canary Islands, and the AI tool I’m using keeps assuming that I will park a rental car for 6 days at the ferry terminal in Los Cristianos while I'm on the island of La Gomera.
    
    Agile teams and coaching on especially hard subjects for AI tools are especially hard because the subject area is so vast. In my office, I have two shelves of books related to Agile and according to DevonThink, another 20GB on my laptop. The more I learn about this subject, the more I realize most answers to questions should be “it depends” and "tell me more".

    ## Highlights

It’s super impressive that agents were able to bootstrap a browser in a week! But holy crap! I hope nobody ever uses that thing or would try to build an actual browser out of it, at least with this generation of agents, it’s still pure slop with little oversight. ([View Highlight](https://read.readwise.io/read/01kfdza76cehr565g7554zs2c9)) ^rw979817858
    - Or maybe some of us are genuinely losing the plot, and we won’t know which camp we’re in until we look back. All I know is that when I watch someone at 3am, running their tenth parallel agent session, telling me they’ve never been more productive — in that moment I don’t see productivity. I see someone who might need to step away from the machine for a bit. And I wonder how often that someone is me.

[^3] Databases/APR Research.dtBase2/Files.noindex/pdf/3d/Introduction to BDD Example Mapping  Cucumber Blog.pdf
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    Introduction to BDD Example Mapping |
    Cucumber Blog
    Clip-Quelle: Introduction to BDD Example Mapping | Cucumber Blog
    Before you pull a user story into development, it’s crucial to have a conversation to clarify
    and confirm the acceptance criteria.
    Some people do this during their backlog refinement or planning poker sessions. Other
    teams have a specific three amigos meeting, specification workshop or discovery
    workshop.
    Whatever you call this conversation, many teams find it hard; it’s unstructured, it takes too
    long and gets boring. The result is they don’t do it regularly or consistently, or maybe they
    just give up on it entirely.
    I’ve discovered a simple, low-tech method for making this conversation short and
    powerfully productive. I call it Example Mapping.
    How it works
    Concrete examples are a tremendous way to help us explore the problem domain, and
    they make a great basis for our acceptance tests. But as we discuss these examples, there
    are other things coming out in the conversation that deserve to be captured too:
    Example Mapping uses a pack of 4-coloured index cards and some pens to capture these
    different types of information as the conversation unfolds. As we talk, we capture them on
    index cards, and arrange them in a map:
    ○ rules that summarise a bunch of examples, or express other agreed constraints
    about the scope of the story.
    ○ questions about scenarios where nobody in the conversations knows what the
    right outcome is. Or assumptions we're making in order to progress.
    ○ new user stories we discovered or sliced and deferred out of scope.
    
    We start by writing the story under discussion on a yellow card and placing it at the top of
    the table.
    Next we write each of the acceptance criteria, or rules that we already know, on a blue
    card and placing those across the table beneath the yellow story card.
    For each rule, we may need one or more examples to illustrate it. We write those on a
    green card and place them under the relevant rule.
    As we discuss these examples, we may uncover questions that nobody in the room can
    answer. We capture those on a red card and move on with the conversation.
    We keep going until the group is satisfied that the scope of the story is clear, or we run out
    of time.
    And that’s it. I told you it was simple!
    Instant Feedback
    As the conversation flows, we quickly build up a visual representation on the table in front
    of us reflecting back our current understanding of the story:
    
    You’ll find that some rules are so obvious you don’t need examples at all. It’s clear from
    the conversation that everyone understands the rule. Great! You can all move on with
    your lives without forcing yourselves to grind out examples like BDD-brainwashed
    automatons.
    Thinking inside the time-box
    A small group of amigos should be able to map out a well-understood, well-sized story in
    about 25 minutes .
    If you can’t, either you’re still getting the hang of this (which is fine), the story is too big
    (definitely not fine), or it still has too much uncertainty in it. Listen to that, and either try
    and slice the story, or let the product person go off and do some homework before you
    put story back into another example mapping session at a later date.
    At Cucumber, we use a quick thumb-vote after 25 minutes to determine whether we think
    the story is ready to pull into development. Even if there are some questions remaining,
    you might think they’re minor enough that you can resolve them as you go. Let the group
    decide.
    Benefits
    Example Mapping helps you zoom in and focus on the smallest pieces of behaviour inside
    your story. By mapping it out you can tease apart the rules, find the core of the behaviour
    you want, and defer the rest until later. With this level of scrutiny, example mapping acts
    like a filter, preventing big fat stories from getting into your sprint and exploding with last-
    minute surprises three days before demo-day.
    It also saves time, and so helps maintain busy product people’s interest in the process.
    ○ A table covered in red (question) cards tells us that we still have a lot to learn
    about this story.
    ○ A table covered in blue (rule) cards tells us that this story is big and complicated.
    Perhaps we can slice it? Take another yellow (story) card and put the sliced story on
    the backlog.
    ○ A rule with many examples might be over-complex. Are there multiple rules at
    play that need to be teased apart?
    
    Many teams assume that the three amigos should write acceptance tests (e.g. Cucumber
    scenarios) during this session, sitting around a projector while someone types formal
    gherkin scenarios into an IDE. There are occasions when this is valuable, but generally I
    think it’s a bad idea. It can actually be distracting from the true purpose of the
    conversation.
    It’s easy to see why people make this mistake: the apparent purpose is to take a user story,
    which already has some pre-defined acceptance criteria , and come up with examples that
    can be turned into acceptance tests .
    I think the true purpose, however, is to reach a shared understanding of what it will take
    for the story to be done. You can move much more quickly towards this goal by staying
    low-tech.
    Friends episodes
    So instead of going for full-blown formal Gherkin scenarios, just try to capture a list of
    rough examples , using the friends episode naming convention.
    For example:
    ○ The one where the customer forgot his receipt
    ○ The one where the product is damaged
    ○ The one where the product was bought 15 days ago

    Many teams assume that the three amigos should write acceptance tests (e.g. Cucumber
    scenarios) during this session, sitting around a projector while someone types formal
    gherkin scenarios into an IDE. There are occasions when this is valuable, but generally I
    think it’s a bad idea. It can actually be distracting from the true purpose of the
    conversation.
    It’s easy to see why people make this mistake: the apparent purpose is to take a user story,
    which already has some pre-defined acceptance criteria , and come up with examples that
    can be turned into acceptance tests .
    I think the true purpose, however, is to reach a shared understanding of what it will take
    for the story to be done. You can move much more quickly towards this goal by staying
    low-tech.
    Friends episodes
    So instead of going for full-blown formal Gherkin scenarios, just try to capture a list of
    rough examples , using the friends episode naming convention.
    For example:
    ○ The one where the customer forgot his receipt
    ○ The one where the product is damaged
    ○ The one where the product was bought 15 days ago

    ## Details
    The New York Times bestseller from Hall of Fame basketball legends Larry Bird and Earvin Magic Johnson. From the moment these two players took the court on opposing sides, they engaged in a fierce physical and psychological battle. Their uncommonly competitive relationship came to symbolize the most compelling rivalry in the NBA. In Celtic green was Larry Bird, the hick from French Lick, with laser-beam focus, relentless determination, and a deadly jump shot, a player who demanded excellence from everyone and whose caustic wit left opponents quaking in their high-tops. Magic Johnson was Mr. Showtime, a magnetic personality with all the right moves. Young, indomitable, he was a pied piper in purple and gold. And he burned with an inextinguishable desire to win. These were the basketball epics of the 1980s — Celtics vs Lakers, East vs West, physical vs finesse, Old School vs Showtime, even white vs black. Each pushed the other to greatness — together Bird and Johnson collected eight NBA Championships, six MVP awards and helped save the floundering NBA at its most critical time. When it started they were bitter rivals, but along the way they became lifelong friends. With intimate, fly-on-the-wall detail, When the Game Was Ours transports readers to this electric era of basketball and reveals for the first time the inner workings of two players dead set on besting one another. From the heady days of trading championships to the darker days of injury and illness, we come to understand Larry’s obsessive devotion to winning and how his demons drove him on the court. We hear him talk with candor about playing through chronic pain and its truly exacting toll. In Magic we see a young, invincible star struggle with the sting of defeat, not just as a player but as a team leader. We are there the moment he learns he’s contracted HIV and hear in his own words how that devastating news impacted his relationships in basketball and beyond. But always, in both cases, we see them prevail. A compelling, up-close-and-personal portrait of basketball’s most inimitable duo, When the Game Was Ours is a reevaluation of three decades in counterpoint. It is also a rollicking ride through professional basketball’s best times.

[^4] MarkPKM/APR/Efforts/Newsletter/2025-02-26-perception-isn-t-reality-and-certainly-not-when-it-comes-to-artificial-intellige.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    ## Technical Factors
    
    Some clever wag will respond that most of the reported code complexity and reduced deployment boils down to the fact that we've ignored the XP Technical Practices for too long. That’s both true and unhelpful, at the same time. The biggest sin by far? Building on Technical Debt without making any effort to remediate it.   
      
    [An excellent paper](https://codescene.com/hubfs/web_docs/Business-impact-of-code-quality.pdf) from the team at CodeScene really brings this home. When the code is already messy and we continue to try to do new feature work or fix a bug, we're 15 times more likely to have defects than if we were working in clean code.   
      
    I love this; when the existing code is messy and we fix a bug, we have a high risk of creating a new bug. Whack-a-mole?  
      
    What other technical factors are there?  
      
    •    Lack of automated test cases (whether Unit Tests or Automated Acceptance Tests) - When code bases have few tests, all changes have higher risk.  
      
    •    Ignoring Test Case Failure - With some troublesome tests, they fail, and the failure isn't easily understood. This should, of course, be a warning that the system is unreliable or, at least, that the test case covers too much. Instead, many teams tag it as ignored and move on.  
      
    •    Long-lived code branches and their partner in crime - Pull Requests are their own hydra. The longer the branch lives, the harder it is to merge into main. (Merge Hell?) The expense of the pull request process and the delays of long-lived branches discourage refactoring. Missed opportunities for refactoring increase our technical debt.  
      
    I could spend an entire workshop day covering this mess. Without delving into solutions, what other technical factors can you think of that affect quality?  
      
    Effective Scrum Teams find where their real bottlenecks are, and then address those problems. AI/LLMs may or may not be included. Just be careful, because using an AI/LLM might give the false sense that you’re making improvements but, without supporting data, it’s likely to be only an illusion, and one that could cost you even greater time and work to overcome.    
      
    Cheers,  
      
    ~ Mark

# Content Ideas

Running list of quick hooks and angles for blog, newsletter, and social. Captured from the Drafts inbox triage. Review periodically and promote the good ones into Writing Tasks (`APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/`).

## Hooks

- **If we implemented every feature in your product backlog today, would your users be happy?** A provocative backlog-as-value question. (captured 2026-06-11)
- **BDD was always about the collaboration.** If you just use Given / When / Then to feed an LLM, it's a prompt with pretty formatting. (BDD + GenAI angle, captured 2026-06-04)
- **GenAI handles computer tasks fine; the more a question touches the real world or human emotions, the less reliable it gets.** (GenAI reliability angle, captured 2026-07-05)
- **Maximizing token budget is silly, going faster doesn't make you more productive.** (AI productivity angle, captured 2026-07-05)
- **Reasoning models don't reason.** Current-generation "reasoning" is statistical pattern matching, replaying patterns from training data, not logical deduction. More effective than non-reasoning models, but still a stochastic parrot. (GenAI reliability angle, captured 2026-02-11)

I'll group them together as a "Scrum/PM scenario bank" to keep the content hooks list clean while still making those scenarios easily accessible.

content.text: Now appending the 20 scenarios as a grouped subsection:

input.old_string: - **Reasoning models don't reason.** Current-generation "reasoning" is statistical pattern matching, replaying patterns from training data, not logical deduction. More effective than non-reasoning models, but still a stochastic parrot. (GenAI reliability angle, captured 2026-02-11)
input.new_string:
- **Reasoning models don't reason.** Current-generation "reasoning" is statistical pattern matching, replaying patterns from training data, not logical deduction. More effective than non-reasoning models, but still a stochastic parrot. (GenAI reliability angle, captured 2026-02-11)

## Scrum / PM scenario bank

Real-world organizational-challenge scenarios, each rich enough for a full post or Scrum-by-Example episode. (captured 2026-01-16 from Drafts triage)

- **Old guard vs new guard.** Veterans refuse to merge until a whole Epic is reviewed; newcomers want frequent merges. Result: merge hell and integration errors.
- **The sunk-cost negotiation trap.** Customer deliberately slows the sales process until the project is ~75% done, then threatens cancellation to force a discount.
- **The "dead horse" retrospective ban.** Management bans recurring external impediments (e.g. a slow third-party supplier) from retrospective discussion.
- **Specialization within a team.** 12 devs, each a one-person show on a separate submodule, so code reviews lack the expertise to be meaningful.
- **The "status pull" efficiency argument.** How to show a manager that whole-team status-report meetings are waste, even when the manager finds them convenient.
- **The "Tom" problem.** A senior dev delivers 80% of a task, overrides the wireframe (green button, not blue), and adds unplanned features like login animations.
- **Revenue-impacting bug priority.** A colleague wants a new "impacts revenue" bug category, making everything crisis-urgent and crowding out other work.
- **Larry vs Winston working hours.** "Laid-back Larry" is stressed by an 8-hour day and needs breaks; "workaholic Winston" feels he's carrying a free-rider.
- **The single-point-of-contact tool conflict.** A contractual single-point-of-contact clause collides with tools (e.g. Basecamp) that invite many-to-many communication.
- **The vicious firefighting cycle.** POs and support constantly pull devs off the Sprint Goal to fix setups or recover data.
- **The zero-sum KPI game.** Engineer's KPI (pass QA bug-free) and tester's KPI (find more bugs) create a conflict of interest that hurts morale.
- **The specialist utilization problem.** An "adopted expert" (e.g. a UX guru) has only ~10% of a Sprint's work but is required at every standup with no outside interruptions.
- **Project vs process in maintenance.** How to define a PM's role when management assigns a PM to a maintenance team whose work has no distinct end.
- **Delayed information from customers.** 60 stories are dev-done but can't be closed because an unresponsive customer has been sitting on needed info for weeks.

  "title": "This will be 30 mins. Get a blank pad or doc ready to capture.",
  "content": "

This will be 30 mins. Get a blank pad or doc ready to capture.

Guidelines: this is only capture--not process or organize. Don't analyze or organize what you write.

**The primary question you are asking yourself is: What do you have ATTENTION on?**

- [ ] Start capturing now. What do you have attention on.
- [ ] Any upcoming meetings you have attention on? Projects?
- [ ] Anything you have attention on w/your spouse, partner, kids, family?
- [ ] Don't worry about figuring out WHAT you're going to do about it. Just capture enough so you'll know what it is when u do process it later.
- [ ] Any health appts. you've been putting off? Annual checkups? Things to check because you've reached a certain age :)
- [ ] If something is already on tasks or projects, write it anyway on your mindsweep. You probably still have your attention on it.
- [ ] Anything w/your gear, equipment, repairs, computer you have attention on?
- [ ] Now look around your office space or wherever you are. What's not EXACTLY the way you want it.

**Don't resist capturing on mindsweep because you're afraid about your workload. You can always park on someday. Or change your standard...**

- [ ] What about your inbox? Sent email box? Scan those to see where your attention has been going.
- [ ] Anything lurking in email folders you have your attention on? Things you've chucked into folders when u were sure you'd see it again?
- [ ] I recommend scanning folders--like sent--because sometimes it will trigger somethingelse. The..."oh that reminds me..." kind of things.
- [ ] How about meetings you've had? Any of you have a graveyard of old meeting notebooks you need to go thru?
- [ ] Now pop over to your calendar. Scan back a few weeks. Then forward a few weeks.
- [ ] Capture as much as you can.
- [ ] Sometimes I'll just write a few key words on the mindsweep, like "Boston event" and move on. Just enuf to capture. 
- [ ] Halloween? Thanksgiving? Christmas? Easter? Birthdays coming up?
- [ ] Gifts to buy? Thank you cards/notes you owe people?
- [ ] Scan in your mind thru your house room by room (or even walk around if u are there).
- [ ] home repairs? how about longer-term stuff w/your house? family? career?

If you look back on your lists and see that most of the things r also on your lists, is what's on your list really the NEXT action?

Things will crawl back into your head if your brain doesn't trust your system is doing a better job

OK folks..coming to the end here. I recommend keep going until you feel done.

  "id": "2C66A05E-32C4-4DE8-96E7-4F102FC59A91",
  "title": "**Government Client: Agricultural Lender**",
  "content": "**Government Client: Agricultural Lender**

** Agile Coach (** **RFR-304)**
Our client requires an **Sr. Agile Coach with extensive Scrum Master experience** to work hands-on with mature Agile delivery teams. 

**Note:** This is not a Project Manager role. Candidates must have demonstrated experience coaching mature Agile teams, advancing their practices, and ingraining Agile principles in how they deliver value.

Remote work from within Canada. 

***Duties Include:***
- Foster the adoption of Agile principles and skills across teams and departments, aligning delivery practices with enterprise strategy. 
- Coach Scrum Masters, Product Owners, and Agile teams to deepen Agile maturity and cultivate high-performing, self-organizing teams. 
- Educate and coach teams and leaders on the uptake and adoption of Agile frameworks (e.g., Scrum, Kanban) tailored to organizational needs. 
- Manage and facilitate Agile ceremonies, workshops, and other key events. 
- Identify and remove systemic impediments to Agile delivery; influence leadership to support change. 
- Develop and manage Agile growth and maturity backlogs, implementation plans, and success metrics. 
- Deliver training to build Agile capability across the organization. 
- Promote a culture of continuous improvement, learning, and collaboration

***Required Experience*****:**
- 8--10 years of experience in Agile environments, including enterprise-level coaching and training. 
- Proven experience with the Scrum and Kanban Agile frameworks. 
- Must have experience coaching mature Agile teams--not teams new to Agile. 
- Must show experience helping long-established Agile teams refine practices, deepen Agile principles, and advance maturity. 
- Experience demonstrating servant leadership and guiding mature teams through continuous improvement cycles. 

***Required Skills*****:**
- Deep expertise in Agile principles, frameworks, and product-centric delivery models. 
- Strong facilitation, mentoring, and communication skills across all organizational levels. 
- Ability to influence change, cross-functional collaboration, resolve complex impediments, and drive strategic alignment. 
- Experience with Agile metrics. 
- Supplemental training on Agile delivery and/or coaching would be considered an asset. 
- Advanced facilitation skills for leading Agile ceremonies, design-thinking workshops, and problem-solving sessions with experienced Agile teams. 
- Ability to measure Agile maturity improvements and articulate how coaching actions improved team value delivery

**Pros**
- It would get me some coaching experience again
- It forces me practice what I preach
- It would get me to engage with people in the real world and not stuck in my own head
- It would allow me to sit out a year of turbulence in the world
- I've a rough idea of the state of the client and they're further along than many in Canada

**Cons**
- What happens to APR? and Heather?
- Would APR ever be to recover from this?
- I would likely be forced to use a company computer in locked down mode

Questions about the job opportunity:
- What happens to my CST and AKT status?
- What is the rate of pay for this position?
- How many hours per week?
- Can I cover off on two workshops for existing clients?
- How many weeks of vacation?

- Find a back channel to figure out what is possible there

  "id": "04D26FA5-21DE-46F8-AD42-6C243E841560",
  "title": "Beyond Prompt Engineering",
  "content": "Beyond Prompt Engineering
The real value of AI isn't speeding existing tasks.  It's solving problems that previously seemed impossible. The AI becomes a thought partner. 

To do this critical thinking is key. The tool becomes a conversational partner not a one off text generator. 

How can I use GenAI to teach people to engage in systems Thinking.  Shallow incorporate into final CSM exercise. Deeper Take pair in notes and use it to help people to learn to understand boundaries 

Realizing that patterns can be applied from out side their original domain will be key. 

LLMs constantly jump to conclusions based on false assumptions. That is another way of restating the critical thinking part

My personal weakness in this while is business is that years of solo work rarely have me reaching out to a tight partner to clarify my ideas earliest happens is when I go to write a blog post. 

**Brainstorming**
AI's have a very different association mechanism and so they won't come up with same ideas as human brainstorming partners. 

**IF...Then** 
Claims that if then analysis exploring from a single hypothesis is important

*I need to do my own reflection and take notes on if then*

https://wulrich.com/csh https://wulrich.com/csh.html consider organizing aI use in degree of difficulty. Start with simple problems and clear guard rails. Build from there. 

Just ask trick. Pass onto the author that in general these tools have no self awareness and so self explanation might be correct or might be hallucinated. 

--
Wrong Template pattern explanation is weak. Models don’t bucket exchanges into categories. When a discussion goes off the rails and it provides generic advice, it seems more likely that either:
- The generic advice was over represented in training data **OR**
- The reward function in the fine tuning, rewarded this behaviour
--
Consider boiling the book down to a set of Claude skills. The book is a set of patterns, I could ask the model to distill the patterns and then turn them into  skills. 

Author also describes apprentice journey which makes me wonder about a map.  
--
Theory of  constraints relates to Liebig's law and also to Amdahls law 

--
Effective Scrum consider giving students access to an AI grounded in our materials and systems Thinking

Also pull in mental models.  Especially reversible vs irreversible. Also complexity. 

A challenge that most people have using AI to help with Scrum and related problems? They're asking the wrong questions",

{
  "id": "5AA5A94F-95BD-45EC-8670-B0EB4085EE02",
  "title": "The core of our discussion today was around two teams that are struggling to perform well. The team lead has been changed for at least one of the teams, and that made a small difference.",
  "content": "The core of our discussion today was around two teams that are struggling to perform well. The team lead has been changed for at least one of the teams, and that made a small difference.  
  
I encouraged the group to engage in Systems Thinking (<https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/systems-thinking/>) to understand some of the many factors that could be contributing to the team's struggles.  
  
In the process, we came up:  

- Not understanding Vision or Strategy (which we have previously identified as an essential issue for all of the teams)  
- Lack of Collaboration - this may stem from a lack of understanding of the value of collaboration: <https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/collaboration-over-work-in-isolation/> or a number of other factors  
- Lack of Psychological Safety, I outlined a safety check: <https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/safety-check/> that could be run with the teams to understand if they have psychological safety.  
- Power Dynamic may be affecting the team both in terms of Psychological Safety and engagement: <https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/why-having-a-tech-lead-or-manager-as-scrum-master-is-a-bad-idea/> in particular, all of the motivational models that I recommend studying, put autonomy in the centre:
    - <https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/motivation/>  

    - <https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/arc-motivational-model/>  

    - <https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/scarf-model/>  
- QA (or other work type) is not my responsibility - in some cases, people feel that they're paid to do development work and helping out QA is not part of their job. *While this is a possible cause, I don't think it is likely*  
- Tyler commented that team members don't feel they have time to pull each other's branches and test their code during the code review process. Further, they commented that they don't have time to write end-to-end tests. *This is likely the key comment*  

**Overcommitment and Missing Definition of Done**  
In response to this, Felipe noted that this felt like a combination of overcommitment in Sprint Planning and an ignored definition of done.  
We touched on the fact that several times, efforts have been made to create a Definition of Done. They are created and then, within a few sprints, ignored and left to gather dust. In my experience, this pattern usually stems from the Definition of Done, being too ambitious for the team's current capabilities and/or capacity.  
  
In addition, taking a leaf from Large Scale Scrum (aka LeSS): <https://less.works/less/framework/definition-of-done> - Felipe suggested that an organization-wide Definition of Done could be created. In the ideal case, this is the right thing to do. Usually, the organization-wide Definition of Done becomes the baseline for the team-level Definition of Done. Teams can exceed it but not fall below it. (This is how we know that the Potentially Releasable Product Increment is of the same quality across the whole organization).  
  
However, in the short term, that may be too far away. If you define an organization-wide Definition of Done, make it clear that this is long-term goal. I used a running or sports analogy to explain the challenge. A team sets a Definition of Done that is too ambitious for their current capabilities. They attempt to meet it for a few sprints, fail and then give up altogether. Instead of this model, I suggested an incremental approach.  
  
Start with a Definition of Done that is achievable for the team, right now. Then, in the next Retrospective, ask the team for the smallest improvement they could make to the Definition of Done towards the long-term goal. During Sprint Planning, remind the team of the Definition of Done, which they committed to and ask them to allocate enough capacity to meet it (i.e. 10--15% of the Sprint). In the rest of Planning, as they commit to Product Backlog Items, ask them to consider the Definition of Done, including the improvements, before they commit to each Product Backlog Item. *In our first couple of Sprints, we care mostly about establishing the self-discipline to pay attention to the Definition of Done and the improvement.* Modify the Sprint Backlog (<https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/>) to include a column for Definition of Done, and a column for the change to Done that the team committed. If the team is struggling during the Sprint, remind them that fewer Product Backlog Items that are truly complete is better than more Product Backlog Items that don't meet the Definition of Done. Go so far as to acknowledge that all of this will affect the team's velocity. If this works, every few Sprints they should master an improvement and then can try the next one.  
  
On the subject of overcommitment, a comment was made about the power dynamic, with the Team Leads committing and the team members having to follow their lead.  
  
My unscientific guess is that improving the Definition of Done, combined with a better understanding of the Vision and Strategy, is going to have the most significant impact on the team's performance.",

Feeling stuck ... t…",
  "content": "More to try to explain (to myself as well as you) why a theme might help us form a structured plan. "Effective Scrum" is a great title for a business program, but it doesn't spark personal visual/literary cues that evoke emotion and interest. "Scrum pain" does. Feeling lost does. Feeling stuck ... these are all "feeling" themes to begin the conversation. "Effective" isn't a feeling, it's a solution to end the initial conversation (by providing a solution). If we use solution wording as our primary message when we're still trying to start the conversation, I question whether it will draw them in as much as if we use feeling wording and THEN end with solution wording. 

That's kind of the "thread" I'm trying to articulate... how we draw them in with one (feeling) message but interweave the wording within the conversation to take them to the end (solution) message of Effective Scrum.

If any of that sparks in your head and makes sense, we could:

1. Pick 3 different themes to apply to our messaging

2. Use a slimmed down version of the existing quiz questions so we're not starting from scratch on that before we even now if people will go to it

3. Make a landing page with the quiz for each theme

4. Post LinkedIn posts with headlines using each theme (I don't yet know whether we should do a batch all one theme, or intersperse the 3 types) pointing to the relevant landing page

5. Do A/B/C testing with the quiz popup (or one week per theme)

6. Also apply the theme in the immediate win that they get at the end of the quiz before leaving the site, and in the follow-up email sequence.

In your note, you set out a new order of doing things with different versions of the quiz/checkup at the top, and I'm not yet seeing the logic of that. I would think the top priority would be finding the secret sauce to get them to come to the quiz. Then once we have that win, it can guide  how to frame everything that follows in a similar wording to what they already responded favourably to, so they stay with us through the remaining process.",

content.text:
{
  "id": "2CEDA8C8-9208-49E3-A45A-41698C68ADCA",
  "title": "Based on the 12 pain points from your documents, here are 5 different Scrum Pain Triage quiz variations:",
  "content": "Based on the 12 pain points from your documents, here are 5 different Scrum Pain Triage quiz variations:

* * *

## **Quiz 1: "The Sprint Killer Assessment"**

**Framing:** What's consistently derailing your sprints?

**Structure:**

- Show all 12 pain points grouped into 3 categories: 
    - **Before Sprint:** Roadmap pivots, vague stakeholder demands, over-commitment
    - **During Sprint:** Mid-sprint changes, cross-team dependencies, technical debt, people not asking for help, daily scrums running long
    - **After Sprint:** Production bugs, retrospectives not fixing issues, story points > customer value, AI code breaks, psychological safety issues

**The Ask:**

1. "Check all that apply to your team"
2. "Which phase causes you the most pain?" (Before/During/After)
3. "Pick your #1 urgent issue right now"

**Result:** Shows their "Sprint Killer Profile" with focus on timing patterns
* * *

## **Quiz 2: "The Hidden Blocker Detector"**

**Framing:** What's the invisible thing slowing your team down?

**Structure:**

- Present 4-5 scenario-based questions with multiple choice
- Each answer maps to 2-3 of your pain points

**Example Questions:**

1. "What happens most often when you think a sprint is going well?"

    - a) External teams tell us they need more time (→ dependencies)
    - b) Stakeholder changes everything mid-sprint (→ scope changes, vague demands)
    - c) Bugs spike in production (→ production bugs, tech debt, AI code issues)
    - d) Team says 'everything's fine' but we miss goals (→ psychological safety, not asking for help)
2. "Where does most of your team's frustration show up?"

    - a) Meetings that drag on (→ daily scrum, retrospectives)
    - b) Same problems every sprint (→ retrospectives, tech debt)
    - c) Constantly changing priorities (→ roadmap pivots, mid-sprint changes)
    - d) Metrics look good but customers aren't happy (→ story points, velocity/bugs)

**Result:** Reveals their "primary blocker pattern" and 2-3 related issues
* * *

## **Quiz 3: "The Scrum Maturity Reality Check"**

**Framing:** Where is your team *really* struggling? (No judgment, just clarity)

**Structure:**

- 3-tier frequency check for each pain point: 
    - **Constantly** (every sprint)
    - **Frequently** (every 2-3 sprints)
    - **Occasionally** (rarely but memorable)
    - **Not our issue**

**The Ask:** Show 8-10 of the most common pain points (skip AI code, over-commitment as they're less universal)

**Scoring Logic:**

- Count number of "Constantly" responses
- If 3+ = "Crisis Mode"
- If 1-2 = "Struggling But Fighting"
- If 0 but 3+ "Frequently" = "Death by 1000 Cuts"

**Result:**

- Shows their maturity stage (not as a score, but as a pattern)
- "Most teams at this stage see improvement by focusing on [their top Constantly issue]"
* * *

## **Quiz 4: "The Team Tension Triage"**

**Framing:** Is this a *people* problem, a *process* problem, or a *systemic* problem?

**Structure:**

- Group the 12 pain points into 3 buckets (pre-categorized for user):

**People & Culture** (4 items to check):
- Team members don't feel safe raising hard truths
- People rarely ask for help when stuck
- Retrospectives find same issues without fixing them
- Story points matter more than customer problems

**Process & Planning** (4 items):
- Mid-sprint scope changes
- Roadmap pivots every quarter
- Daily scrum runs over 15 minutes
- Stakeholders' demands are vague

**System & Technical** (4 items):
- Cross-team dependencies derail work
- Technical debt blocks new features
- Production bugs spike despite velocity
- AI-generated code quietly breaks

**The Ask:**

1. "Check all that apply in each category"
2. "Which category has the most checks?"
3. "Pick your most urgent issue overall"

**Result:** Shows their "primary tension point" (People/Process/System) with explanation of why these cluster together
* * *

## **Quiz 5: "The 90-Second Scrum Check"**

**Framing:** How broken is your Scrum *really*? (The fastest reality check)

**Structure:**

- Single page, visual checklist
- 12 pain points shown as simple yes/no statements
- Real-time counter at top: "You've identified X issues"

**The Twist:** After they check items, ONE final question: **"If you could only fix ONE of these in the next 30 days, which would give your team the biggest relief?"**

(Forces prioritization from everything they checked)

**Result Logic:**

- 1-3 checked: "Targeted Pain" → Tactical fixes
- 4-6 checked: "Systemic Strain" → Need strategic approach
- 7+ checked: "Drowning in Dysfunction" → Need triage support
- PLUS their #1 priority gets a custom "Start Here" guide
* * *

## **My Recommendation:**

**Start with Quiz #5 ("90-Second Scrum Check")** because:

1. **Fastest** - respects busy ScrumMasters/managers
2. **Dead simple** - just check boxes
3. **Forces prioritization** - the final question is where the magic happens

  "content": "Based on the 12 pain points from your documents, here are 5 different Scrum Pain Triage quiz variations:

* * *

## **Quiz 1: "The Sprint Killer Assessment"**

**Framing:** What's consistently derailing your sprints?

**Structure:**

- Show all 12 pain points grouped into 3 categories: 
    - **Before Sprint:** Roadmap pivots, vague stakeholder demands, over-commitment
    - **During Sprint:** Mid-sprint changes, cross-team dependencies, technical debt, people not asking for help, daily scrums running long
    - **After Sprint:** Production bugs, retrospectives not fixing issues, story points > customer value, AI code breaks, psychological safety issues

**The Ask:**

1. "Check all that apply to your team"
2. "Which phase causes you the most pain?" (Before/During/After)
3. "Pick your #1 urgent issue right now"

**Result:** Shows their "Sprint Killer Profile" with focus on timing patterns
* * *

## **Quiz 2: "The Hidden Blocker Detector"**

**Framing:** What's the invisible thing slowing your team down?

**Structure:**

- Present 4-5 scenario-based questions with multiple choice
- Each answer maps to 2-3 of your pain points

**Example Questions:**

1. "What happens most often when you think a sprint is going well?"

    - a) External teams tell us they need more time (→ dependencies)
    - b) Stakeholder changes everything mid-sprint (→ scope changes, vague demands)
    - c) Bugs spike in production (→ production bugs, tech debt, AI code issues)
    - d) Team says 'everything's fine' but we miss goals (→ psychological safety, not asking for help)
2. "Where does most of your team's frustration show up?"

    - a) Meetings that drag on (→ daily scrum, retrospectives)
    - b) Same problems every sprint (→ retrospectives, tech debt)
    - c) Constantly changing priorities (→ roadmap pivots, mid-sprint changes)
    - d) Metrics look good but customers aren't happy (→ story points, velocity/bugs)

**Result:** Reveals their "primary blocker pattern" and 2-3 related issues
* * *

## **Quiz 3: "The Scrum Maturity Reality Check"**

**Framing:** Where is your team *really* struggling? (No judgment, just clarity)

**Structure:**

- 3-tier frequency check for each pain point: 
    - **Constantly** (every sprint)
    - **Frequently** (every 2-3 sprints)
    - **Occasionally** (rarely but memorable)
    - **Not our issue**

**The Ask:** Show 8-10 of the most common pain points (skip AI code, over-commitment as they're less universal)

**Scoring Logic:**

- Count number of "Constantly" responses
- If 3+ = "Crisis Mode"
- If 1-2 = "Struggling But Fighting"
- If 0 but 3+ "Frequently" = "Death by 1000 Cuts"

**Result:**

- Shows their maturity stage (not as a score, but as a pattern)
- "Most teams at this stage see improvement by focusing on [their top Constantly issue]"
* * *

## **Quiz 4: "The Team Tension Triage"**

**Framing:** Is this a *people* problem, a *process* problem, or a *systemic* problem?

**Structure:**

- Group the 12 pain points into 3 buckets (pre-categorized for user):

**People & Culture** (4 items to check):
- Team members don't feel safe raising hard truths
- People rarely ask for help when stuck
- Retrospectives find same issues without fixing them
- Story points matter more than customer problems

**Process & Planning** (4 items):
- Mid-sprint scope changes
- Roadmap pivots every quarter
- Daily scrum runs over 15 minutes
- Stakeholders' demands are vague

**System & Technical** (4 items):
- Cross-team dependencies derail work
- Technical debt blocks new features
- Production bugs spike despite velocity
- AI-generated code quietly breaks

**The Ask:**

1. "Check all that apply in each category"
2. "Which category has the most checks?"
3. "Pick your most urgent issue overall"

**Result:** Shows their "primary tension point" (People/Process/System) with explanation of why these cluster together
* * *

- Single page, visual checklist

[^1] Databases/APR Research.dtBase2/Files.noindex/pdf/2/flowmetricsforscrumteams.pdf
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    Chapter 1 - Let’s Begin 5
    finished point–might be fairly straightforward in Scrum: just map
    your finished point to what your Definition of Done (DoD) requires.
    In other words, most of the time the finished point in your Scrum
    workflow would be any time you’ve added one or more PBIs to
    your Increment and that Increment has met your Definition of
    Done (DoD).
    But what if your initial DoD does not include (a) that the Increment
    was shipped, (b) that once shipped value was validated, or (c) that
    the value feedback is incorporated into future decision making?
    And what if our customer wants answers to “when will it be done”
    in each of those cases? The Scrum solution would be to change
    your Scrum Team’s DoD so that it does include those extra criteria
    (remember your Scrum Team can always raise the quality outlined
    in the organization’s DoD–you just can’t lower it to below the
    organizational standard). However, organizational constraints may
    prevent you from changing your team’s DoD to be much broader in
    scope (e.g., your team is not allowed to deploy code to production).
    The beauty is that in this instance Scrum is not restrictive; rather,
    it is fairly flexible.
    Figure 1.1 - Example Workflow
    When using Scrum, there is nothing stopping you from defining a
    workflow where work finishes after your given DoD has been met.
    (This is where we get into the discussion of “Done” vs. “Done Done”
    vs. “Done Done Done” etc.) For example, in the above workflow
    (Options -> Discovery -> Building -> Validating -> Done), let’s say
    that (and we’re not saying this is a good idea) the Scrum Team
    is only involved in the “Building” step and that the DoD only
    addresses Increments that come out of the Building phase. If this
    were the case, then nowhere in Scrum does it say only measure
    what happens in Building. Nothing is stopping you from measuring
    through to Done, or through to Validating, or just through Building.

[^2] Databases/APR Research.dtBase2/Files.noindex/pdf/c/less-for-mark-levison.pdf
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    62
    3. Adoption
    2. Define “Done:
    A better and stronger Definition of Done (DoD or “done”) requires a
    broader skill set within the teams. For example, if performance testing is
    included in the DoD, then the teams need to acquire that skill. It can be
    acquired by learning, but often it is acquired by moving a person with
    performance-testing skill from his specialized performance testing
    group into the team. On the other hand, if performance testing is
    excluded from the DoD, then the separate performance-testing group
    will stay and operate the same way as before, until the DoD is expanded.
    Therefore…
    And a weaker DoD causes additional risk and delay! We explore all
    these topics further in the Definition of Done chapter.
    see Definition of
    Done chapter
    The effect on the amount of organizational change makes the DoD a critical
    management tool for LeSS adoption . Managers need to make a trade-off
    between a strong DoD, leading to more organizational change and less
    delay and risk, and a weak DoD, leading to less organizational change
    and increased risk and delay. The key question is, “ How much change can
    my organization handle at this time ?”
    3. Have Appropriately Structured Teams
    Each Team has a shared responsibility for achieving their common goal.
    To support their success, ensure that each Team is appropriately struc-
    tured. Requirements for the initial teams:
    > dedicated —each person is a member of one and only one team
    > stable —the members of the team aren’t changed frequently
    > long-lived —the team isn’t a temporary project team but stays
    together for years
    A better and stronger Definition of Done results in
    more organizational change (eliminating groups,
    roles, positions, …) than a poorer and weaker one.
    https://less.works For Mark Levison only, id:mark-levison
    
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    73
    LeSS Huge
    • LeSS HUGE Rules •
    Guide: Evolutionary Incremental Adoption
    LeSS adoptions are best done all-at-once, but LeSS Huge adoptions
    must be done evolutionary and incrementally. There are two
    approaches to LeSS Huge adoptions:
    Guide: Feature-
    Team Adoption
    Maps, p. 90
    > Gradual incremental adoption over the whole product group.
    All the teams gradually improve their scope and capability at the
    same pace. This could be by expanding the product-level Defini-
    tion of Done and using tools such as feature team adoption maps.
    > Focused deeper adoption at a part of the product group.
    Improvements focus to make a few teams really good, and then
    spread one team at the time. This might be by expanding a few
    teams’ Definition of Done, letting them work on specific improve-
    ment items, and by focused coaching.
    Both approaches work. The impatient gradual incremental adoption has
    the advantage of hopefully having faster product-wide results, though it
    often doesn’t happen because all teams need to solve the same prob-
    lems at the same time—causing new problems. The focused deeper
    adoption seems slower but avoids pain in all teams. The drawback, of
    course, is that the already existing pain won’t be resolved as they aren’t
    (yet) the focus of the adoption.
    The LeSS adoption principles suggest a preference to the focused
    deeper adoption, which is covered here. The gradual incremental adop-
    tion is covered in the Organizing by Customer Value chapter.
    LeSS Huge adoptions, including the structural changes, are
    done with an evolutionary incremental approach.
    Remember each day: LeSS Huge adoptions take many months
    or years, infinite patience, and a sense of humor.
    https://less.works For Mark Levison only, id:mark-levison
    
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    230
    10. Definition of Done
    Don’t confuse the Definition of Done with acceptance criteria; the lat-
    ter are conditions a specific item has to fulfill to be shipped. “Fulfilling all
    acceptance criteria” is usually included in the Definition of Done.
    L E SS D ONE
    These days, a one-team product group should be able to have a perfect
    Definition of Done and might even be able to continuously deliver
    during the Sprint. But for many large product groups, a perfect Defini-
    tion of Done feels impossible while they still measure stabilization peri-
    ods in months. Bas remembers being surprised when he received a
    bonus for some code he had written two years earlier. The product had
    finally shipped.
    When scaling, these principles are related to Definition of Done:
    Transparency —In traditional large groups, visibility is often attempted
    by installing additional management control and reporting. LeSS groups
    have a clear, shared Definition of Done and an integrated product at
    least at the end of each Sprint. This creates real, painfully clear trans-
    parency.
    Continuous Improvement towards Perfection —What to improve?
    The gradual expansion of the Definition of Done gives direction to
    improvements and their measures.
    https://less.works For Mark Levison only, id:mark-levison
    
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    243
    LeSS Huge
    Is an organization with a perfect Definition of Done done with improv-
    ing? No, improvements won’t ever be done. They never stop. Further
    improvement can be made:
    > Have shorter Sprints.
    > Release many times during a Sprint.
    > Expand the Definition of Done beyond potentially shippable, and
    include market success in the Definition of Done. In this case, an
    item is not done until you have a measurement about how custom-
    ers are using it. The Lean Startup framework refers to this as vali-
    dated learning .
    L E SS H UGE
    There are no Huge-specific rules or guides. One shared Definition of
    Done is applicable for the whole product, across all Requirement Areas.
    https://less.works For Mark Levison only, id:mark-levison
