{
  "id": "965AD1B1-A2FA-4A92-8C51-FF3BED328C93",
  "title": "Teams that are struggling to perform.",
  "content": "Teams that are struggling to perform.

The core of our discussion today was around two teams that are struggling to perform well. The team lead has been changed for at least one of the teams, and that made a small difference.

I encouraged the group to engage in Systems Thinking (https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/systems-thinking/) to understand some of the many factors that could be contributing to the team's struggles.

In the process, we came up:
- Not understanding Vision or Strategy (which we have previously identified as an essential issue for all of the teams)
- Lack of Collaboration - this may stem from a lack of understanding of the value of collaboration: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/collaboration-over-work-in-isolation/ or a number of other factors
- Lack of Psychological Safety, I outlined a safety check: https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/safety-check/ that could be run with the teams to understand if they have psychological safety.
- Power Dynamic may be affecting the team both in terms of Psychological Safety and engagement: https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/why-having-a-tech-lead-or-manager-as-scrum-master-is-a-bad-idea/ in particular, all of the motivational models that I recommend studying, put autonomy in the centre:
	- https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/motivation/
	- https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/arc-motivational-model/
	- https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/scarf-model/
- QA (or other work type) is not my responsibility - in some cases, people feel that they're paid to do development work and helping out QA is not part of their job. *While this is a possible cause, I don't think it is likely*
- Tyler commented that team members don't feel they have time to pull each other's branches and test their code during the code review process. Further, they commented that they don’t have time to write end-to-end tests. *This is likely the key comment*

## Overcommitment and Missing Definition of Done
In response to this, Felipe noted that this felt like a combination of overcommitment in Sprint Planning and an ignored definition of done.

We touched on the fact that several times, efforts have been made to create a Definition of Done. They are created and then, within a few sprints, ignored and left to gather dust. In my experience, this pattern usually stems from the Definition of Done, being too ambitious for the team's current capabilities and/or capacity.

In addition, taking a leaf from Large Scale Scrum (aka LeSS): https://less.works/less/framework/definition-of-done - Felipe suggested that an organization-wide Definition of Done could be created. In the ideal case, this is the right thing to do. Usually, the organization-wide Definition of Done becomes the baseline for the team-level Definition of Done. Teams can exceed it but not fall below it. (This is how we know that the Potentially Releasable Product Increment is of the same quality across the whole organization).

However, in the short term, that may be too far away. If you define an organization-wide Definition of Done, make it clear that this is long-term goal. I used a running or sports analogy to explain the challenge. A team sets a Definition of Done that is too ambitious for their current capabilities. They attempt to meet it for a few sprints, fail and then give up altogether. Instead of this model, I suggested an incremental approach.

Start with a Definition of Done that is achievable for the team, right now. Then, in the next Retrospective, ask the team for the smallest improvement they could make to the Definition of Done towards the long-term goal. During Sprint Planning, remind the team of the Definition of Done, which they committed to and ask them to allocate enough capacity to meet it (i.e. 10-15% of the Sprint). In the rest of Planning, as they commit to Product Backlog Items, ask them to consider the Definition of Done, including the improvements, before they commit to each Product Backlog Item. *In our first couple of Sprints, we care mostly about establishing the self-discipline to pay attention to the Definition of Done and the improvement.* Modify the Sprint Backlog (https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/) to include a column for Definition of Done, and a column for the change to Done that the team committed. If the team is struggling during the Sprint, remind them that fewer Product Backlog Items that are truly complete is better than more Product Backlog Items that don’t meet the Definition of Done. Go so far as to acknowledge that all of this will affect the team’s velocity. If this works, every few Sprints they should master an improvement and then can try the next one.

On the subject of overcommitment, a comment was made about the power dynamic, with the Team Leads committing and the team members having to follow their lead.

My unscientific guess is that improving the Definition of Done, combined with a better understanding of the Vision and Strategy, is going to have the most significant impact on the team's performance.

{
  "id": "9E2137BD-4A22-4809-AFF9-3FAC5319A723",
  "title": "Why ChatGPT et al don't make a good agile coach",
  "content": "Why ChatGPT et al don't make a good agile coach

// Origin story - Joe Foley at the AgileAlliance posted a toot about using to 
The Agile Manifesto Challenge is a simple, focused exercise: for one week, apply the Agile Manifesto values and 12 Principles in your daily work with prompts and assistance from our AI Agile coach.

On AI tool use I'm neither for or against. I have more experience than most in the Agile Community: [https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/category/artificial-intelligence/](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/category/artificial-intelligence/) -- I think the often missed point is that we fail to examine the second order effects of our actions. Ironically this is why I'm replying to you in the first place.

The problem with your suggestion we're missing context. If you ask any LLM for advice on Agile or some other subject you know well, your questions will be thoughtful and come from a place of knowledge. Further you have enough experience to recognize bad ideas when you see them.

I've meet somewhere over 8000 people in the past 15yrs, who're attempting to get better using some flavour Agile. Most ppl ask questions that are five rungs down the ladder …..

For example the classic questions might be:  
- How can I make my team go faster? Or   
- Doesn't Agile mean we change business strategy every Sprint?  
…

The questions are reasonable given the popular understanding of Agile. However the people asking these questions don't have the experience to recognize good or bad responses.

In addition given the quality of the average Agile advice on internet, we need ask what have the models encoded? The best advice or ???

. In your original example had you written a longer item i,e, a blog post and explored some examples of using ChatGPT with a several specific questions that would have been more helpful. This would demonstrate to the reader nuance and depth required to use these tools well.  
….and there is still a risk.

There are much deeper challenges with models in general. These are tools, whose only job is to produce the next plausible response to a prompt.

Potential Issues:  
- Run the same query - 10 times with same model, are all responses close enough for good coaching advice?  
- Turn on/off reasoning mode - what affect did this have?  
- Try running the same query different models, maybe you use OpenAI/ChatGPT and I use Anthrophic/Claude and Google/GeminiFlash. Are the results stable?  
- Is the query set large enough to predict behaviour in the general case? Listening a podcast with the co-founder of Weights and Biases he talked about teams running 1000s of test cases as they fine tune models. To test an AI Coach the same would need to be done.

In the hands of someone who already has deep knowledge a general chat model can make a great tool for reflective thinking? In the hands of someone with limited Agile experience the risks seem to far out weigh the benefits.
",

{
  "id": "5759AE4D-BC5C-4975-A1D3-BC80D4746459",
  "title": "Five Ladder of Importance Belief Systems for Sarah",
  "content": "# Five Ladder of Importance Belief Systems for Sarah

## 1. Ladder of Importance: What Makes Scrum Ceremonies Effective

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Understanding the *purpose* of each ceremony
**Second Rung:** Team psychological safety to speak up
**Third Rung:** Clear outcomes and action items from each ceremony
**Fourth Rung:** Time-boxing and facilitation techniques
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Following the "correct" ceremony format/structure

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah believes that if her team understood *why* they're doing ceremonies, everything else would fall into place. If you're selling her tools for better time-boxing while she's struggling with purpose, she won't hear you.

---

## 2. Ladder of Importance: What Creates Team Productivity

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Clarity on what problem we're solving (the "why")
**Second Rung:** Reducing dependencies and impediments
**Third Rung:** Team skill level and cross-functionality
**Fourth Rung:** Sprint planning accuracy
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Velocity metrics and burndown charts

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah believes productivity starts with clarity of purpose, not measurement. Selling her velocity tracking tools addresses her least important concern, not her biggest pain point.

---

## 3. Ladder of Importance: What Makes a Good ScrumMaster

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Ability to identify and address systemic issues
**Second Rung:** Creating space for team self-organization
**Third Rung:** Coaching skills and empathy
**Fourth Rung:** Knowledge of Scrum practices
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Scrum certification credentials

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah already has her certification but feels ineffective. She's looking for diagnostic skills and systemic thinking, not more certifications. She's at the bottom of the ladder, yearning for the top.

---

## 4. Ladder of Importance: What Drives Product Success

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Building the *right* thing (product discovery)
**Second Rung:** Understanding customer problems deeply
**Third Rung:** Fast feedback loops with users
**Fourth Rung:** Quality code and technical practices
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Shipping features on schedule

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah is frustrated when stakeholders change priorities mid-sprint because they're focused on the bottom rung (schedule) while she believes the top rung (building the right thing) should drive decisions.

---

## 5. Ladder of Importance: What Enables Team Improvement

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Team ownership of problems and solutions
**Second Rung:** Making underlying patterns visible (systems thinking)
**Third Rung:** Small, consistent experiments
**Fourth Rung:** Good retrospective facilitation
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Following improvement frameworks (like OKRs, action item lists)

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah's retrospectives feel ineffective because her team isn't taking ownership. She's trying to fix this with better facilitation (fourth rung), but the real issue is at the top - the team doesn't own the improvement process.

  "title": "Five Ladder of Importance Belief Systems for Sarah",
  "content": "# Five Ladder of Importance Belief Systems for Sarah

## 1. Ladder of Importance: What Makes Scrum Ceremonies Effective

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Understanding the *purpose* of each ceremony
**Second Rung:** Team psychological safety to speak up
**Third Rung:** Clear outcomes and action items from each ceremony
**Fourth Rung:** Time-boxing and facilitation techniques
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Following the "correct" ceremony format/structure

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah believes that if her team understood *why* they're doing ceremonies, everything else would fall into place. If you're selling her tools for better time-boxing while she's struggling with purpose, she won't hear you.

---

## 2. Ladder of Importance: What Creates Team Productivity

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Clarity on what problem we're solving (the "why")
**Second Rung:** Reducing dependencies and impediments
**Third Rung:** Team skill level and cross-functionality
**Fourth Rung:** Sprint planning accuracy
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Velocity metrics and burndown charts

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah believes productivity starts with clarity of purpose, not measurement. Selling her velocity tracking tools addresses her least important concern, not her biggest pain point.

---

## 3. Ladder of Importance: What Makes a Good ScrumMaster

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Ability to identify and address systemic issues
**Second Rung:** Creating space for team self-organization
**Third Rung:** Coaching skills and empathy
**Fourth Rung:** Knowledge of Scrum practices
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Scrum certification credentials

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah already has her certification but feels ineffective. She's looking for diagnostic skills and systemic thinking, not more certifications. She's at the bottom of the ladder, yearning for the top.

---

## 4. Ladder of Importance: What Drives Product Success

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Building the *right* thing (product discovery)
**Second Rung:** Understanding customer problems deeply
**Third Rung:** Fast feedback loops with users
**Fourth Rung:** Quality code and technical practices
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Shipping features on schedule

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah is frustrated when stakeholders change priorities mid-sprint because they're focused on the bottom rung (schedule) while she believes the top rung (building the right thing) should drive decisions.

---

## 5. Ladder of Importance: What Enables Team Improvement

**Top Rung (Most Important):** Team ownership of problems and solutions
**Second Rung:** Making underlying patterns visible (systems thinking)
**Third Rung:** Small, consistent experiments
**Fourth Rung:** Good retrospective facilitation
**Fifth Rung (Least Important):** Following improvement frameworks (like OKRs, action item lists)

*Marketing Insight:* Sarah's retrospectives feel ineffective because her team isn't taking ownership. She's trying to fix this with better facilitation (fourth rung), but the real issue is at the top - the team doesn't own the improvement process.

{
  "id": "6C7A33DD-A889-4ABD-99CA-B6D1BE474AA0",
  "title": "Copilot and Quarterly Review and Planning",
  "content": "Copilot and Quarterly Review and Planning
(This would also work for the weekly reviews)

I'm using Copilot (https://www.obsidiancopilot.com/en) to help find things I've missed in my quarterly review and planning.

I continue to do my quarterly and weekly reviews, by hand. I'm using copilot as a final check to see what I might have missed.

I see the major value of a review process, as a form of reflection. Taking the time to think about the week or quarter is the value of the process. Taking time to see the big picture is why I do it.

I start the review process, by consolidating all of my daily and weekly journal entries into a pair of markdown files. quarterly_days and quarterly_weeks. I do this because, it is easier to scroll two long files, than >100 individual files. (90 days + 14 weeks).

My review process is loosely based on David Spark's aka MacSparky's
https://www.macsparky.com/blog/2022/01/personal-retreat-video-and-planning-pdf/ -- my template for this is at the bottom of this note.

After each section (i.e Opening Prompts, Roles Audit, Improve in the Next 90 days), I ask Copilot to review my work in that section and compare it to the quarterly_days and quarterly_weeks, I ask for bullet points of things I might have missed. These files are just temporary objects, to speed my review process and I delete them when I’m done.

I find the GeminiPro 2.5 model is good choice for me, as it can handle a much larger context window than the other Claude - my normal choice. (I find the Anthropic Claude models are more empathetic and better at distilling nuance from personal reflections).

## Prompt examples:
- Please find any mentions of actions or activities that wasted my time or energy.
- Looking at [[2025-Q4]] what important themes have i missed that are mentioned in my notes? 
- Look at "Improve in the next 90 days" - does it address the areas mentioned above? Does it cover issues raised in [[quaterly_weeks]] and [[quaterly_days]]?

## Sample output
*   **Mobile Games:** You specifically mention playing "stupid amounts of Suduko" and later deleting the game ([[quaterly_weeks]], 2025-W32), as well as playing Mahjong and Wurdweb, which you describe as "infinity games" and a form of avoidance ([[quaterly_weeks]], 2025-W34; [[quaterly_days]], 2025-09-17, 2025-09-25).
*   **Social Media & Aimless Browsing:** You mention "lots of flipping through social media" ([[quaterly_weeks]], 2025-W34) and cycling through email, LinkedIn, and Mastodon throughout the day ([[quaterly_days]], 2025-08-14). You also describe falling down "a dozen rabbit holes" looking up old friends or browsing forums about cameras ([[quaterly_days]], 2025-07-04, 2025-08-19).

*Caveat - some of the things it finds are very helpful. Much it surfaces notes I've already taken or is outright wrong. Don't trust the output*

(I will likely create my own plugin to automate turining daily and weekly journal entries into long markdown files)

- What was my biggest win of the last quarter? what are the things you have achieved that make you the proudest?
- What was the biggest lesson learned in the last quarter?

- What were the most delightful moments of the last quarter?
- What challenges did I face in the last quarter?
- What are the current areas of focus and progress that make you the most confident?

  "id": "972AC70A-38FC-4BCD-8886-312D4AD32521",
  "title": "I get too many newsletters, to read every week and yet some of them contain nuggets. Sometimes I want to read them in the next week and sometimes I want to be able to find again later.",
  "content": "I get too many newsletters, to read every week and yet some of them contain nuggets. Sometimes I want to read them in the next week and sometimes I want to be able to find again later.

My goal is to summarize each newsletter with GenAI and turn it into a digest, links to each newsletter and bullet points outlining the content. (No turgid AI generated prose).

(My email is handled by Gmail, however I'm in the process of looking for a replacement, so I don't to link back to Gmail).

Goal
- Once a week, produce a digest of the newsletters I’ve received that week.

Current Manual Workflow:
- file newsletters into a Gmail folder /WeeklyNewsletters 

Once a week:
- In AppleMail and drag the newsletters into DevonThink
- In DevonThink - Select all the newsletters and use an AI to summarize (currently using Gemini 2.5 Pro -  it has a large context window and does a good enough job of summarizing the content)
- Copy and paste the summaries into Markdown document in Obsidian

Ideally, I would like to automate all of this.

Desired Automations
- **AppleMail -> DevonThink** - AppleMail's rules only work if the is still in the inbox. Hpw can I automate moving newsletters from /WeeklyNewsletters to DevonThink? 
- **DevonThink Summarisation** - SmartRules can be triggered once a week. I can’t figure out how to get smart to scan all of the newsletters at the same time and send the output to a Markdown file.
- **DevonThink -> Obsidian** - Export the generated Markdown to file in Obsidian.

I'm not even sure the right place to ask some of these questions ;-)

1. Mid-sprint "urgent" scope changes

3. Daily Scrum routinely runs over 15 minutes

4. Retrospectives find the same issues without fixing them

8. Production bugs spike even though velocity looks great


====

I HAVE NO IDEA (YET) HOW I'LL TACKLE THEM
5. Stakeholders' demands are so vague they can’t be met

6. Story Points matter more than solving customer problems

7. People rarely ask for help when stuck

9. Team members don’t feel safe raising hard truths

10. Technical debt consistently blocks new feature work

====

DON'T HAVE PEERDRAFT URLS YET
11. Cross‐team dependencies routinely derail your work
12. You waste time fixing AI-generated code that breaks later

- use of // comments to get my attention works well

  "content": "Let’s start a thread about use cases. Very good idea. Collaboration is more fun. (As a scrum educator this is core to my world. 

https://discord.com/channels/1182847556032659546/1413630728398176306/1413632965887660032

Hey Mark, thanks for joining. Apologies in advance i might be replying intermittently for now but will definitely reply. 

My thought process to design a workflow usually begins with a certain objective i want to achieve and then seeing if using AI is actually going to be an efficient/better approach or suitable for the task. 

Co-pilot is actually a tool that I combine alongside other incredible obsidian plugins and Zapier sometimes to achieve my objective. But you could say Co-Pilot really is a high quality engine driving the workflow. 

With that in mind, what's your thought process like ? Do we align? And what are some tasks or objectives that you're thinking AI might be able to help with. Let me know 🙂

I will share in a moment some of the things I use Copilot for in my day to day life and work.
--
https://discord.com/channels/1182847556032659546/1413630728398176306/1413639192801448018

My usecases:
__**1) High quality Semantic Searches**__
- I use Claude Sonnet 4 and Voyage-3-large as an embedding model

__** Medical**__
- I'm of a medical background hence accuracy is critical for my semantic searches
- I incorporate a combination of notes and curated textbooks to create drafts for lecture notes, study cards, information leaflets using co-pilot vault semantic search
- I also like to discuss questions with this dataset to revise/explore/learn a new topic/ challenge my understanding about a certain concept.

**__Finance__**
- I'm a value investor so I also utilise Co-pilot to conduct deep research and draft personalised stock reports using prompts - to aid me in decision making.
- I also use additional plugins to aid with the task
- A brief demo of this was here https://discord.com/channels/1182847556032659546/1405680249097814086/1405711690426880050

__**Writing**__
- Similar to the example above; I use co-pilot alongside other obsidian plugins to draft  inspiring and informative leaflets or short pamphlets about topics that matter to me , for e.g. current events, technology, medical topics etc.

- Or to perform semantic searches for other areas in life like religion, history, politics etc.

**__2) Project mode:__**
- Knowledge bot : I convert some books into knowledge bots so I can talk to the book for insights and discuss ideas or even to help with a task. It's like having the author guide me with work or do the work for me. So I've created like an Editor-in-chief bot, a debating bot and a work bot where I upload relevant notes and materials from work for quickly recalling a certain process or workflow I need to refresh my memory about.

- I even used the editor-in-chief and some knowledge bots to help me create a strong cover letter for a job application for instance. 

Theres more usecases - but these are the common things I use for now. I'm always reading the usecase-showcase section to get inspired too.

My suggestion to discovering usecases - is find a few things you're interested in, but dont have the time or direction to explore further and use AI to help you get the conversation started and develop the idea. 

I believe AI works best with humans at the centre guiding it than the other way around. And Co-Pilot, aptly named, is doing a smashing job at that in my view.

https://discord.com/channels/1182847556032659546/1413630728398176306/1413641866552803409

__**3) Integration with workflow automation tools**__
- This has by far been the hottest trend in AI of late and my increasing usecase
- Using Zapier - I am able to automate a lot of workflows. For example I'm subscribed to many newsletters that flood my inbox and a lot of times I'm guilty of never having read them. 

So 've created automations where the moment an email from a certain newsletter lands in my inbox, a summary gets created and appended to a google doc , the email gets deleted (moved to trash can) and then I get notifed of WhatsApp that the document has been appended with a link to the google doc. I then click the link to review the summary and if i want to read further - ill pick the email out of the trash can and explore. I can also ofcourse manually erase sections of the summary once I've read it allowing me to "clear the cache" so to speak.

Doing so has allowed me to finally remain better synced up with news that matter to me. This is just one simple automation example developed based on something that makes my life easier and helps me achieve a certain goal.

- Another one is for example everytime i get emailed an invoice from accounts - the PDF is automatically renamed and uploaded to a specific cloud folder and email deleted. 
- Another one is when I receive emails from various senders - I have AI create a draft response which I can then edit and send off - so the bulk of the work is already done. 

I have highlighted the plethora of use cases that users can achieve by connecting Co-Pilot to these workflow automation tools like Zapier and N8N here. https://discord.com/channels/1182847556032659546/1395400296087163030

Do open up the PDF (also generated using Co-Pilot and usecases verified by me) to get some ideas 🙂

https://discord.com/channels/1182847556032659546/1413630728398176306/1413643678374953032

One other tip I can suggest to get ideas - make a voice recording talking about what you do, what you want to achieve at work and in life, talk a little bit about details of how you think you can achieve it and then save this recording. 

Convert that recording to text (using STT like whisper plugin on obsidian - or any you fancy). 

Then save that text as an MD file. 

Then attach that MD file as context in copilot search. Use a strong model like Claude Sonnet 4/ Gemini 2.5 Flash with token limit set to max (65000) and then write a query:

*"Based on the file attached, give me some ideas on how I can leverage AI to aid me with the task, and also any other helpful goals that might be relevant to what I'm trying to achieve."*

And then just follow that conversation, save it as a new note with appropriate headings and subheadings using composer tool - and there you go you have your first idea/insight. Maybe hashtag it with something. Then keep asking, keep noting, tagging and progressing. 

That's sort of been my process sometimes in the early days. Nowadays it's a bit more goal oriented and refined.

Found 4 file source(s). Cite using [^n] with no gaps.

[^1] MarkPKM/APR/Efforts/Blog/Will AI Make the Federal Government More Efficient or Just More Busy?.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    The Prime Minister of Canada told federal government to become more efficient and cut their budgets, and it’s suggested that artificial intelligence can play a key role.(https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/#footnotes)
    
    I know AI, I have seen the inside workings of many government departments, and I know something about efficiency. All politics aside (no, really), I have concerns. Using AI isn’t a bad idea, but it needs to be approached in a responsible way. _Especially_ if you’re the federal government.
    
    _Oxford English Dictionary: **efficiency** (-shensi) n. State or quality of being efficient; (Mech. & Phys.) ratio of useful work done to total energy expended or heat taken in;_
    
    Be careful, a focus on efficiency can make systems worse. We save a few dollars, but slow down the whole system. “Do more with less” reduces quality and eventually costs more.
    
    There are two major kinds of “AI” in use today. GenerativeAI and PredictiveAI. Generative AI is the tool most of us are familiar with (ChatGPT, Claude, etc). We write some text, and the model _generates_ a response. PredictiveAI attempts to _predict_ future events based on past data — for example, in an emergency department, deciding who needs hospital admission for pneumonia and who can recover at home.
    
    Can either of these tools help make the federal government more efficient?
    
    - GenAI is excellent at creating a large body of text or other content quickly. GenAI promises that it will speed up many tasks, allowing each worker to get more stuff done.
    - PredictiveAI makes many promises, including automating decision-making.
    
    Will either of these make departments more efficient? Assuming GenAI made everyone faster (it doesn’t) and that it didn’t make mistakes (it does), we expect GenAI to speed up departments magically so they can generate more “stuff”. Lots of stuff makes it seem like people are busy. Busy might appear to be efficient, but those aren’t synonymous.
    
    The problem is the [bottlenecks](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/bottlenecks/). You know them from the daily commute, that place on the highway where it always slows down. The only place to improve is the bottleneck itself (see [Theory of Constraints](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/theory-of-constraints/) for more details). So even if GenAI does speed up individual workers, unless that person is the bottleneck, the most likely outcome is that it will make the logjam worse.
    
    ![[Attachments/d7df316cc1f69515f4f01de0d4dd1a31_MD5.jpg]]
    
    sketch of GenAI making stuff faster, but with a bottleneck
    
    Even if we magically fixed one bottleneck (example: issuing passports), there might be consequences (e.g. issuing emergency travel documents for Canadians stuck overseas). Without a clear set of priorities, we might make the whole system worse.
    
    I’ve seen inside many federal government departments, agencies, and crown corporations. I’ve seen departments where the work has already been approved. The work item should take 15-20 days of working time, and it spends 75-90 days waiting for additional management decision-making. In this case, the bottleneck is the speed of decision-making and the lack of autonomy. All but the smallest decisions need to get approval from a senior manager; this is a side effect of a risk-averse culture. The manager demands more information to make each decision, so team members are pulled off their current work to find that information. The number of decisions managers are expected to make is overwhelming, so many vital decisions wait on their desks for weeks or months. If people use GenAI simply to create more quantity rather than quality, it will increase the number of decisions that managers need to make, snowballing the problem.
    
    If decisions are waiting for months, can we responsibly use PredictiveAI to speed the process? In theory, maybe. But in practice, PredictiveAI makes decisions based on past data, and that can lead to poor predictions when the training data was incomplete, or it was biased, or future conditions don’t match the past. Even if PredictiveAI was good at making forecasts of what will happen in thousands of cases (it isn’t), that predictive value is useless at making each single decision (e.g. Should we send this specific patient home?) In these cases, it’s no better than flipping a coin.[[2]](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/#footnotes)
    
    Finally, the focus on efficiency creates other problems. When everything is about efficiency, the focus is primarily on the cost of the work. Missing from the equation: are we doing the right job? Is the work being done well? Efficiency creates systems that are fragile, with many handoffs that are slower at delivering results.
    
    Over years of making mistakes, I’ve learned what does work:
    
    - Define what results matter and have clear priorities. Most groups can sustain only three priorities, max, at one time. Overall priorities matter, so when there is a conflict it needs to be clear which item(s) must be finished first.
    - Study the flow of the system. The easiest way is to build a [Kanban](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/kanban/) board and see where work gets stuck or spends time waiting. Find the bottleneck and consider how to improve throughput there.
    - Push decision-making down to people doing the work. Most decisions are reversible, and so are lower cost. Reversible choices can be made with less information and less authority… and, therefore, less delays.
    
    Can GenAI help? Perhaps once we’ve found the bottleneck. Some work can be sped up with GenAI but most valuable work still requires a thoughtful person. Instead of chasing magic promises, [bottlenecks](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/bottlenecks/) are most often solved by asking people to help out with the work.

[^3] MarkPKM/APR/Efforts/Newsletter/2026-07-21-unintended-ai-experiments-150-agents-2-useful-insights.md
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    The past couple of weeks have been full, between wildfire smoke and the elimination of England from the World Cup. I attended a Cycling Canada - cycling skill course (CAN-BIKE 4). I've been riding a bike for over 50 years. I assumed that I knew a lot. There was much to learn about how cars see (and don’t see) cyclists, how to participate in a group ride and survive Ottawa traffic. For once, I won't try to find a clever Agile analogy from this. GenAI gives me plenty to noodle on, so let's go there instead.
    
    If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried, you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI-related topics in this issue, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).
    
    ## Canadian Government AI Strategy
    Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means building more data centres and investing in Canadian AI companies.
    
    The real problem is that the strategy defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny. I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person who created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.
    
    The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on it, in [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).
    
    Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.
    
    I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. I think existing machine learning will be rebranded as AI.
    
    ## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
    In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: next week's model (Fable) will solve all the existing problems and use agents to offset other agents mistakes (Opus).
    
    I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App I’m building. I accidentally used agents with Claude Opus when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.
    
    ### Fable Security Audit
    Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to have Fable do an audit.     GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.
    
    Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction.     The Prime Minister of Canada told federal government to become more efficient and cut their budgets, and it’s suggested that artificial intelligence can play a key role.(https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/#footnotes)
    
    I know AI, I have seen the inside workings of many government departments, and I know something about efficiency. All politics aside (no, really), I have concerns. Using AI isn’t a bad idea, but it needs to be approached in a responsible way. _Especially_ if you’re the federal government.
    
    _Oxford English Dictionary: **efficiency** (-shensi) n. State or quality of being efficient; (Mech. & Phys.) ratio of useful work done to total energy expended or heat taken in;_
    
    Be careful, a focus on efficiency can make systems worse. We save a few dollars, but slow down the whole system. “Do more with less” reduces quality and eventually costs more.
    
    There are two major kinds of “AI” in use today. GenerativeAI and PredictiveAI. Generative AI is the tool most of us are familiar with (ChatGPT, Claude, etc). We write some text, and the model _generates_ a response. PredictiveAI attempts to _predict_ future events based on past data — for example, in an emergency department, deciding who needs hospital admission for pneumonia and who can recover at home.
    
    Can either of these tools help make the federal government more efficient?
    
    - GenAI is excellent at creating a large body of text or other content quickly. GenAI promises that it will speed up many tasks, allowing each worker to get more stuff done.
    - PredictiveAI makes many promises, including automating decision-making.
    
    Will either of these make departments more efficient? Assuming GenAI made everyone faster (it doesn’t) and that it didn’t make mistakes (it does), we expect GenAI to speed up departments magically so they can generate more “stuff”. Lots of stuff makes it seem like people are busy. Busy might appear to be efficient, but those aren’t synonymous.
    
    The problem is the [bottlenecks](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/bottlenecks/). You know them from the daily commute, that place on the highway where it always slows down. The only place to improve is the bottleneck itself (see [Theory of Constraints](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/theory-of-constraints/) for more details). So even if GenAI does speed up individual workers, unless that person is the bottleneck, the most likely outcome is that it will make the logjam worse.
    
    ![[Attachments/d7df316cc1f69515f4f01de0d4dd1a31_MD5.jpg]]
    
    sketch of GenAI making stuff faster, but with a bottleneck
    
    Even if we magically fixed one bottleneck (example: issuing passports), there might be consequences (e.g. issuing emergency travel documents for Canadians stuck overseas). Without a clear set of priorities, we might make the whole system worse.
    
    I’ve seen inside many federal government departments, agencies, and crown corporations. I’ve seen departments where the work has already been approved. The work item should take 15-20 days of working time, and it spends 75-90 days waiting for additional management decision-making. In this case, the bottleneck is the speed of decision-making and the lack of autonomy. All but the smallest decisions need to get approval from a senior manager; this is a side effect of a risk-averse culture. The manager demands more information to make each decision, so team members are pulled off their current work to find that information. The number of decisions managers are expected to make is overwhelming, so many vital decisions wait on their desks for weeks or months. If people use GenAI simply to create more quantity rather than quality, it will increase the number of decisions that managers need to make, snowballing the problem.
    
    If decisions are waiting for months, can we responsibly use PredictiveAI to speed the process? In theory, maybe. But in practice, PredictiveAI makes decisions based on past data, and that can lead to poor predictions when the training data was incomplete, or it was biased, or future conditions don’t match the past. Even if PredictiveAI was good at making forecasts of what will happen in thousands of cases (it isn’t), that predictive value is useless at making each single decision (e.g. Should we send this specific patient home?) In these cases, it’s no better than flipping a coin.[[2]](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/#footnotes)
    
    Finally, the focus on efficiency creates other problems. When everything is about efficiency, the focus is primarily on the cost of the work. Missing from the equation: are we doing the right job? Is the work being done well? Efficiency creates systems that are fragile, with many handoffs that are slower at delivering results.
    
    Over years of making mistakes, I’ve learned what does work:
    
    - Define what results matter and have clear priorities. Most groups can sustain only three priorities, max, at one time. Overall priorities matter, so when there is a conflict it needs to be clear which item(s) must be finished first.
    - Study the flow of the system. The easiest way is to build a [Kanban](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/kanban/) board and see where work gets stuck or spends time waiting. Find the bottleneck and consider how to improve throughput there.
    - Push decision-making down to people doing the work. Most decisions are reversible, and so are lower cost. Reversible choices can be made with less information and less authority… and, therefore, less delays.
    
    Can GenAI help? Perhaps once we’ve found the bottleneck. Some work can be sped up with GenAI but most valuable work still requires a thoughtful person. Instead of chasing magic promises, [bottlenecks](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/bottlenecks/) are most often solved by asking people to help out with the work.

    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    ## Evaluating Chatbots in the Context of Agile Coaching
    In [[Why AI Doesn't Replace Your ScrumMaster]] I shared my list of criteria for evaluating the use of AI tools in general. Two of the questions are particularly relevant here:
    - **Purpose**: Do we understand the activity or task we're attempting to improve with the AI tool? *I don't think most people deploying a chatbot have a deep understanding of how it will be used*
    - **Risk Tolerance**: Can we afford the errors the tool will make? Do we know the subject area well enough to sufficiently review and identify errors in the generated work? *This is the big risk. A general user asks a question of the AI Chatbot about Story Points or JIRA. They get indifferent or outright bad advice. They don’t have the expertise to know that the advice was bad, so they implement it.*
    
    NOTE BLOCK CONTENT:
    ## Other Risks to Be Aware of with AI Chatbots
    Not all models are good at sticking to your content. If it doesn't find the answer in your content, many models will draw on their training data to answer the question. I can promise you that the average training data doesn’t have good advice for Agile teams.
    
    AI vendors have reduced hallucinations (i.e. making stuff up) recently, but randomness and, therefore, hallucinations are inherent to the technology. More subtly, sometimes the chatbot just gets confused and forgetful. For example, I'm planning a hiking vacation in the Canary Islands, and the AI tool I’m using keeps assuming that I will park a rental car for 6 days at the ferry terminal in Los Cristianos while I'm on the island of La Gomera.
    
    Agile teams and coaching on especially hard subjects for AI tools are especially hard because the subject area is so vast. In my office, I have two shelves of books related to Agile and according to DevonThink, another 20GB on my laptop. The more I learn about this subject, the more I realize most answers to questions should be “it depends” and "tell me more".
    
    Critical Thinking is key with these tools, and yet, as Microsoft demonstrated with a 2025 paper[^1], the better the tool sounds, the more likely people are to believe the output.
